chem_edx.9.0.summary: Chemists identify metal ions (cations) with two simple tests. A **flame test** identifies lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper(II) ions from the colour they give to a blue Bunsen flame, because heated electrons in the ions give out light of particular colours. Adding **sodium hydroxide solution** makes many metal ions form coloured or white insoluble hydroxide precipitates, which identify aluminium, calcium, copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions, while ammonium ions release **ammonia gas** on warming, which turns damp red litmus paper blue. You must be able to describe each method, give each result and write balanced ionic equations.

core.h: What a cation test is for
core.p: A salt is made of a positive ion (cation) and a negative ion (anion). To identify an unknown salt you test for each ion separately. This spec point covers the **cations**: the metal ions Li+, Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, plus the non-metal cation ammonium, NH4+. Each test must give a result that is **unique** (only one ion gives it) and easy to see.
bullets: **Flame tests** are used for Li+, Na+, K+, Ca2+ and Cu2+.
**Sodium hydroxide solution** is used for Al3+, Ca2+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and NH4+.
Ca2+ and Cu2+ can be identified by **both** methods, which is useful for confirming a result.
Na+ and K+ hydroxides are soluble, so these ions give **no precipitate** with NaOH and must be found by flame test.
A qualitative test tells you **which** ion is present, not how much of it there is.
Tests can be done on a solid (flame test) or on a solution of the solid in distilled water (sodium hydroxide test).

callouts.p: A positively charged ion, formed when an atom or group of atoms loses electrons.
Group 1 ions (Li+, Na+, K+): flame test only. Transition metal ions (Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+) and Al3+: sodium hydroxide. Ca2+ and Cu2+: either test. NH4+: sodium hydroxide plus warming, then test the gas.

core.p: When a metal ion is heated strongly in a flame, its electrons gain energy and jump up to **higher energy levels** (shells further from the nucleus). They are unstable there and quickly drop back down, giving out the extra energy as **light**. The energy gaps between the shells are different for every element, so each metal ion gives out its own particular colours of light.
bullets: Heat energy from the flame **excites** electrons to higher energy levels.
Electrons fall back to lower energy levels and **emit light energy**.
The size of the energy drop fixes the colour (wavelength) of the light.
Because each element has a different arrangement of energy levels, each ion gives a **characteristic** flame colour.
This is also the basis of flame photometry and emission spectra (a separate spec point).

callouts.p: If asked why different metals give different colours, say the electron energy levels are different in each element, so the energy (and colour) of light emitted is different.

core.h: How to carry out a flame test
core.p: A flame test needs a clean wire loop, a blue Bunsen flame and a small sample of the solid. The **cleaning step** is essential, because any ions left on the wire from an earlier test would give a false colour.
bullets: Use a loop of **nichrome** (or platinum) wire. These metals are unreactive and do not colour the flame themselves.
**Clean the wire**: dip it in concentrated hydrochloric acid, then hold it in a hot blue Bunsen flame. Repeat until the wire gives **no colour** to the flame.
Dip the clean wire into the acid again so the solid sample sticks to it, then dip it into the **solid sample**.
Hold the loop in the **edge of a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame**, with the air hole open.
**Observe and record** the colour of the flame.
Clean the wire again before testing a different sample.
Safety: concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive, so wear eye protection and take care near the hot flame.

callouts.p: A yellow (safety) flame already has its own yellow-orange colour, which would hide the colour of the ion. Always open the air hole to get a blue flame.
Mark schemes reward: clean nichrome wire with conc. HCl, dip in sample, place in blue (non-luminous) Bunsen flame, observe colour, compare to known colours.

core.h: Flame test colours you must learn
core.p: Edexcel expects these five flame colours. Learn the exact words, because the mark scheme is strict about them: for example, lithium is **red** (crimson) and calcium is **orange-red**, so just writing "red" for calcium will not score.
bullets: Lithium, Li+: **red** (crimson red).
Sodium, Na+: **yellow** (strong, bright yellow-orange).
Potassium, K+: **lilac** (pale purple).
Calcium, Ca2+: **orange-red** (brick red).
Copper(II), Cu2+: **blue-green** (green).
The test identifies the **metal ion**, not the whole compound: copper(II) sulfate and copper(II) chloride both give a blue-green flame.

callouts.p: Li-Red, Na-Yellow, K-Lilac (K and L sit next to each other in the alphabet), Ca-Orange-red, Cu-Blue-green.

core.p: If a sample contains a **mixture of metal ions**, the flame test may not work well, because the colour of one ion can **mask** (hide) the colour of another. Sodium is the worst offender: even a tiny amount of sodium impurity gives such a strong yellow flame that it swamps the pale lilac of potassium.
bullets: Masking means one bright flame colour **hides** a weaker one.
Example: a mixture of sodium and potassium ions gives a yellow flame, so potassium may be missed.
Sodium compounds are very common impurities (for example from sweat on fingers), so the wire must be **clean** and handled carefully.
A blue cobalt glass filter can be used to absorb the yellow light so the lilac of potassium can be seen (useful background, not required).
Flame tests therefore work best on a **single pure compound**.
Instrumental methods such as flame photometry can identify the ions in a mixture (separate spec point).

callouts.p: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used in a flame test, some flame colours can be masked.

core.p: Many metal hydroxides are **insoluble** in water. When sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of a metal salt, hydroxide ions (OH-) join with the metal ions to form a solid metal hydroxide. This solid appears as a cloudy **precipitate**, and its colour identifies the metal ion.
bullets: Dissolve a small amount of the solid in **distilled water** (tap water contains ions that could interfere).
Put about 1 cm depth of the solution into a test tube.
Add **dilute sodium hydroxide solution a few drops at a time** using a dropping pipette.
Observe the **colour of any precipitate** formed.
Then add **excess** sodium hydroxide solution and observe whether the precipitate dissolves. This is how Al3+ is told apart from Ca2+.
Safety: sodium hydroxide is corrosive (irritant when dilute), so wear eye protection.

callouts.p: An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed and react.
Add the NaOH slowly at first. If you pour in a lot at once, the white aluminium hydroxide precipitate may form and dissolve again so quickly that you never see it.

core.p: Each metal ion gives a precipitate of a particular colour. Iron is the classic exam pair: **iron(II) gives green** and **iron(III) gives brown**, so the test tells you the charge on the iron ion as well as the metal.
bullets: Aluminium, Al3+: **white precipitate**, which **dissolves in excess** NaOH to give a **colourless solution**.
Calcium, Ca2+: **white precipitate**, which does **not** dissolve in excess NaOH.
Copper(II), Cu2+: **blue precipitate**.
Iron(II), Fe2+: **green precipitate** (dirty or pale green). On standing in air it slowly turns orange-brown at the surface as it is oxidised to iron(III).
Iron(III), Fe3+: **brown precipitate** (orange-brown or red-brown).
Sodium, potassium and lithium ions: no precipitate, because their hydroxides are soluble.

callouts.p: Al3+ and Ca2+ both give a white precipitate. Add excess NaOH: aluminium hydroxide dissolves, calcium hydroxide does not. A flame test also works: Ca2+ gives orange-red, Al3+ gives no characteristic colour.

core.p: The precipitation reactions only involve the metal ion and the hydroxide ion. The other ions (such as Na+ and SO4 2-) do not change, so they are **spectator ions** and are left out of the ionic equation. To balance it, use **one OH- for each positive charge** on the metal ion.
bullets: Aluminium: Al3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Al(OH)3(s)
Calcium: Ca2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Ca(OH)2(s)
Copper(II): Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s)
Iron(II): Fe2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)2(s)
Iron(III): Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s)
The precipitate always has the state symbol **(s)**; the ions are **(aq)**.
Full equation example: CuSO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s) + Na2SO4(aq)

callouts.p: An ionic equation must balance both atoms and charge. For Fe3+ + 3OH-: total charge on the left is 3+ and 3- = 0, and Fe(OH)3 is neutral, so it balances.

core.h: Why aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess
core.p: Aluminium hydroxide is **amphoteric**: it can react with both acids and bases. When more sodium hydroxide is added, the hydroxide ions react with the solid aluminium hydroxide to form a soluble ion, so the white precipitate disappears and a **colourless solution** is left. Calcium hydroxide is not amphoteric, so it stays as a precipitate.
bullets: Al(OH)3(s) + OH-(aq) → [Al(OH)4]-(aq)
The product, the aluminate ion, is soluble and colourless.
This is the **only** precipitate in this spec point that dissolves in excess NaOH.
So: white precipitate that dissolves = Al3+; white precipitate that stays = Ca2+.

callouts.p: Say the precipitate dissolves to form a colourless solution. Clear means see-through and could be coloured, so it may not be credited.

core.p: Ammonium ions (NH4+) do not form a precipitate with sodium hydroxide. Instead, on **warming**, they react with hydroxide ions to release **ammonia gas**. The gas is then identified because it is alkaline: it turns **damp red litmus paper blue**.
bullets: Add sodium hydroxide solution to the solid or solution in a test tube.
**Warm gently** using a Bunsen burner (do not boil, as the solution may spit).
Hold a piece of **damp red litmus paper** (or damp universal indicator paper) at the **mouth of the test tube**, without touching the sides.
If ammonium ions are present, ammonia gas is given off and turns the paper **blue**.
Ammonia also has a sharp, choking smell, but you must never smell gases directly to identify them in the lab.
Ionic equation: NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l)

callouts.p: The litmus paper must be damp because ammonia has to dissolve in water to form hydroxide ions (NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-), which is what changes the colour. Dry paper will not change colour.
If the litmus touches the side of the tube it may pick up sodium hydroxide solution, which is alkaline and would turn it blue even without ammonia.

core.p: Real exam questions often give you a set of observations and ask you to name the ion. Work through the evidence in order: flame colour first, then the NaOH precipitate colour, then what happens in excess. Using two tests that agree makes the identification **more certain**.
bullets: Blue-green flame + blue precipitate with NaOH = **copper(II), Cu2+**.
Orange-red flame + white precipitate that stays in excess = **calcium, Ca2+**.
No flame colour + white precipitate that dissolves in excess = **aluminium, Al3+**.
Yellow flame + no precipitate = **sodium, Na+**.
Lilac flame + no precipitate = **potassium, K+**.
Green precipitate = **Fe2+**; brown precipitate = **Fe3+** (iron gives no characteristic Edexcel flame colour).
Gas turning damp red litmus blue on warming with NaOH = **ammonium, NH4+**.

callouts.p: Write copper(II) ion or Cu2+, iron(III) ion or Fe3+. Writing just iron or copper loses the mark when the charge matters.

core.h: Advantages and limits of these chemical tests
core.p: Chemical tests are cheap, quick and need only simple apparatus, which is why they are used in school labs. However, they rely on a person judging colours and they only work well on pure samples, which is why industry often uses instrumental methods instead.
bullets: **Advantages**: simple, cheap, quick, little equipment needed.
**Limitations**: colour judgement is subjective (orange-red and red can look similar).
Flame colours can be **masked** in mixtures.
Small amounts of an ion may not give a visible result (tests are not very **sensitive**).
Tests only tell you **which** ion is present, not its **concentration**.
Contamination (dirty wire, tap water) can give **false positives**.

callouts.p: To decide a colour, compare the result with a known sample of the ion tested under the same conditions.

analogy.t: Ion tests are like a police line-up with fingerprints
analogy.p: Each suspect (ion) leaves a unique fingerprint: a flame colour or a precipitate colour. The detective (you) matches the mark found at the scene against a known record to name the suspect. Two different kinds of evidence (flame test and NaOH test) that point to the same suspect make the case stronger. The analogy breaks down because ions are not hiding anything: the colours come from real chemistry (electrons emitting light, or an insoluble hydroxide forming), and some 'fingerprints' can be smudged over by another suspect, which is masking, something real fingerprints do not do in the same way.

terms.d: A positive ion, such as Na+, Cu2+ or NH4+.
A test that identifies some metal ions from the colour they give to a blue Bunsen flame.
An unreactive alloy wire used to hold the sample in a flame test because it gives no flame colour of its own.
A flame colour that belongs to one particular metal ion and so identifies it.
When the flame colour of one ion hides the colour of another ion in a mixture.
An electron that has gained energy and moved to a higher energy level.
Light given out when excited electrons fall back to lower energy levels.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react together.
A compound of a metal ion and hydroxide ions, such as Cu(OH)2; many are insoluble and coloured.
More of a reagent than is needed to react with all of the other substance.
Able to react with both acids and bases; aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric so it dissolves in excess NaOH.
An equation showing only the ions and substances that change in a reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An ion present in the mixture that does not take part in the reaction.
The positive ion NH4+, identified by warming with NaOH to release ammonia gas.
An alkaline gas, NH3, that turns damp red litmus paper blue.
A test that shows which substance is present but not how much.

mistakes.w: Calcium gives a red flame.
mistakes.r: Calcium gives an orange-red flame; red (crimson) is lithium.

mistakes.w: Potassium gives a purple flame.
mistakes.r: Potassium gives a lilac flame.

mistakes.w: Iron(II) gives a brown precipitate and iron(III) gives green.
mistakes.r: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate; iron(III) gives a brown (orange-brown) precipitate.

mistakes.w: Clean the wire with water.
mistakes.r: Clean the nichrome wire by dipping in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heating in a blue flame until there is no colour.

mistakes.w: Hold the sample in a yellow flame.
mistakes.r: Use a blue (non-luminous, roaring) Bunsen flame so its own colour does not hide the ion's colour.

mistakes.w: Aluminium hydroxide precipitate goes clear in excess.
mistakes.r: The white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution.

mistakes.w: Test for ammonia with dry litmus paper / blue litmus paper.
mistakes.r: Use damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.

mistakes.w: Cu2+ + OH- → CuOH
mistakes.r: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s): one OH- for each positive charge.

mistakes.w: Sodium ions give a white precipitate with NaOH.
mistakes.r: Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so there is no precipitate; identify Na+ with a flame test (yellow).

exam.q: State the colour of the flame produced by potassium ions in a flame test.
model: Lilac.
exam.tip: Purple or violet may not be accepted. Learn lilac.

exam.q: Give the flame test colour of lithium ions and of calcium ions.
model: Lithium: red (crimson).
Calcium: orange-red.
exam.tip: Be precise. Red for calcium scores nothing.

exam.q: Describe how to carry out a flame test on a solid sample.
model: Clean a nichrome (or platinum) wire loop by dipping in concentrated hydrochloric acid and holding in a flame until no colour is seen.
Dip the wire in the solid sample.
Hold the sample in a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame.
Observe the colour of the flame and compare it with known colours.
exam.tip: Cleaning the wire is the mark most often missed.

exam.q: A student does a flame test on a mixture of sodium chloride and potassium chloride. Explain why the student may not see the lilac colour.
model: The yellow colour of sodium ions is very bright.
It masks (hides) the lilac colour of the potassium ions.
exam.tip: Use the word masks.

exam.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of iron(III) chloride. State what is seen.
model: Brown (orange-brown) precipitate.
exam.tip: Always say precipitate, not just the colour.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between iron(II) ions and hydroxide ions.
model: Fe2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)2(s): correct formulae and balancing.
Correct state symbols.
exam.tip: Match OH- to the charge on the metal ion.

exam.q: Two solutions each give a white precipitate when a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution are added. Describe how you would use sodium hydroxide to show which contains aluminium ions and which contains calcium ions.
model: Add excess sodium hydroxide solution to each.
The precipitate that dissolves (forms a colourless solution) contains aluminium ions.
The precipitate that does not dissolve contains calcium ions.
exam.tip: The key word is excess.

exam.q: Describe a test to show that a solid contains ammonium ions.
model: Add sodium hydroxide solution and warm.
Hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the test tube.
The litmus turns blue (ammonia gas is given off).
exam.tip: Damp and red are both needed.

exam.q: Explain why a metal ion gives a coloured flame when heated.
model: Electrons gain energy from the flame and move to higher energy levels.
Electrons fall back to lower energy levels.
Energy is given out as light of a particular colour (because energy levels differ for each element).
exam.tip: Mention energy levels, not just electrons getting hot.

exam.q: A white solid X gives a blue-green flame. A solution of X gives a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution. Identify the cation in X and write the ionic equation for the precipitate forming.
model: Copper(II) ion, Cu2+.
Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s)
Correct state symbols.
exam.tip: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is white, so a white solid can still contain Cu2+.

exam.q: Devise a plan using flame tests and sodium hydroxide solution to identify which of four unlabelled solids contains each of these ions: Li+, Na+, Fe2+ and Fe3+.
model: Clean a nichrome wire in concentrated hydrochloric acid and a blue flame until there is no colour.
Do a flame test on each solid in a blue Bunsen flame, cleaning the wire between samples.
Red (crimson) flame shows Li+; yellow flame shows Na+.
Dissolve the other two solids in distilled water and add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise.
Green precipitate shows Fe2+.
Brown (orange-brown) precipitate shows Fe3+.
exam.tip: A 6 mark plan needs both the method and the expected results for every ion.

worked.q: An unknown salt gives an orange-red flame. A solution of the salt gives a white precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, and the precipitate stays when excess is added. Identify the cation and write the ionic equation.
steps: Orange-red flame suggests calcium ions.
White precipitate could be Al3+ or Ca2+.
Precipitate does not dissolve in excess, so it is not aluminium.
Both tests agree: calcium ion, Ca2+.
Each Ca2+ has a 2+ charge, so it needs 2OH-: Ca2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Ca(OH)2(s).
worked.ans: Calcium ion, Ca2+. Ca2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Ca(OH)2(s).

worked.q: Aluminium sulfate solution is tested with sodium hydroxide. Describe what is seen as the sodium hydroxide is added drop by drop and then in excess, and write equations for both stages.
steps: Stage 1: hydroxide ions combine with Al3+ to form insoluble aluminium hydroxide, seen as a white precipitate.
Al3+ has a 3+ charge so it needs three OH-: Al3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Al(OH)3(s).
Stage 2: aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric and reacts with more OH-.
Al(OH)3(s) + OH-(aq) → [Al(OH)4]-(aq), a soluble colourless ion.
So the precipitate dissolves to give a colourless solution.
worked.ans: A white precipitate forms, then dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution. Al3+ + 3OH- → Al(OH)3, then Al(OH)3 + OH- → [Al(OH)4]-.

worked.q: A student warms an unknown white solid with sodium hydroxide solution and holds dry blue litmus paper over the tube. Nothing happens, and the student concludes no ammonium ions are present. Evaluate this conclusion.
steps: Ammonia is an alkali, so it turns red litmus blue. Blue litmus stays blue in alkali, so no change would be seen anyway.
The paper was dry: ammonia must dissolve in water on the paper to produce OH- ions and change the colour.
So the test could not have shown ammonia even if it was present.
Improve: repeat with damp red litmus paper held at the mouth of the tube, not touching the sides.
worked.ans: The conclusion is not valid; the test should be repeated with damp red litmus paper, which turns blue if ammonium ions are present.

chem_edx.9.1.summary: Negative ions (anions) are identified with simple chemical tests that each give one unmistakable result. **Carbonate ions** fizz with dilute acid, giving carbon dioxide that turns limewater milky. **Sulfate ions** give a white precipitate of barium sulfate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution. **Halide ions** give coloured silver halide precipitates with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution: white for chloride, cream for bromide and yellow for iodide. Grade 9 answers also explain why each acid is added first and why the wrong acid would ruin the test.

core.p: An **anion** is a negative ion. In a salt it is paired with a cation, so a full identification needs a cation test and an anion test. Edexcel requires tests for five anions: **carbonate (CO3 2-)**, **sulfate (SO4 2-)**, **chloride (Cl-)**, **bromide (Br-)** and **iodide (I-)**. Each test adds a reagent that reacts with only that anion to give a gas or an insoluble precipitate you can see.
bullets: Carbonate: add **dilute acid**, test the gas with **limewater**.
Sulfate: add **dilute hydrochloric acid**, then **barium chloride solution**.
Halides: add **dilute nitric acid**, then **silver nitrate solution**.
Tests are done on a solution of the solid in **distilled water** (the carbonate test also works on the solid).
Each test is **qualitative**: it shows which ion is present, not how much.

callouts.p: A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom or group of atoms gains electrons.

core.p: Carbonates react with acids to make a salt, water and **carbon dioxide** gas. The fizzing alone is not proof, because other reactions also give gases, so the gas must be **bubbled through limewater** to confirm it is carbon dioxide.
bullets: Place a small amount of the solid (or its solution) in a test tube.
Add a few cm3 of **dilute hydrochloric acid** (any dilute acid works).
Observe **effervescence** (fizzing, bubbles of gas).
Quickly fit a bung and **delivery tube** and bubble the gas through **limewater** (calcium hydroxide solution).
If the limewater turns **milky (cloudy white)**, the gas is carbon dioxide, so a carbonate is present.
Alternative: draw the gas up with a teat pipette and bubble it through limewater in a second tube.

callouts.p: Metals such as magnesium fizz with acid too, but they give hydrogen. Only the limewater result proves the gas is carbon dioxide.

core.h: Carbonate test: equations and why limewater goes milky
core.p: In the acid, hydrogen ions react with carbonate ions to form carbon dioxide and water. In the limewater, carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form **calcium carbonate**, which is insoluble and makes the solution look milky.
bullets: Ionic equation: CO3 2-(s or aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l)
Example: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
Example: Na2CO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
Limewater: Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)
The tiny particles of white solid **calcium carbonate** make the limewater cloudy.
Two H+ ions are needed because the carbonate ion has a **2- charge**.

callouts.p: Carbonate: effervescence with dilute acid; the gas turns limewater milky (cloudy).
Say milky or cloudy for limewater. Do not say the limewater turns white and solid, or that it turns cloudy and then clear, unless the question asks about excess CO2.

core.p: Sulfate ions react with **barium ions** to form **barium sulfate**, a white solid that is very insoluble. The sample is first acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution is added.
bullets: Put about 2 cm3 of the solution in a test tube.
Add a few drops of **dilute hydrochloric acid**.
Add a few drops of **barium chloride solution**, BaCl2(aq).
A **white precipitate** shows that sulfate ions are present.
Ionic equation: Ba2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Example: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) → BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
Safety: barium chloride is **toxic**, so wear eye protection and avoid contact; wash hands afterwards.

callouts.p: Sulfate: add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution; a white precipitate (barium sulfate) forms.

fig.cap: Figure 2: Test for sulfate ions in three steps. The sample solution is acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid (which removes carbonate ions), then barium chloride solution is added. A white precipitate of barium sulfate shows sulfate ions are present.

core.h: Why add dilute hydrochloric acid first?
core.p: This is a favourite grade 9 question. **Carbonate ions** also react with barium ions to form **barium carbonate**, which is also a white precipitate. That would give a **false positive**. Adding dilute hydrochloric acid first destroys any carbonate ions by turning them into carbon dioxide gas, so any white precipitate that then forms must be barium sulfate.
bullets: Without acid: Ba2+(aq) + CO3 2-(aq) → BaCO3(s), a white precipitate that looks just like BaSO4.
The acid reacts with carbonate: CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O, removing it.
Barium sulfate does **not** dissolve in or react with dilute acid, so the sulfate result is unaffected.
**Do not use dilute sulfuric acid** to acidify: it contains sulfate ions, so it would always give a white precipitate, even if the sample had none.
Dilute nitric acid would also work, but hydrochloric acid is the reagent Edexcel names with barium chloride.

callouts.p: If a question says a student added sulfuric acid then barium chloride, the conclusion is invalid because the acid itself provided sulfate ions.

core.p: Chloride, bromide and iodide ions all form **insoluble silver halides** with silver ions. The colour of the precipitate tells you which halide is present. The solution is first acidified with dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution is added.
bullets: Put about 2 cm3 of the solution in a test tube.
Add a few drops of **dilute nitric acid**, HNO3(aq).
Add a few drops of **silver nitrate solution**, AgNO3(aq).
**Chloride, Cl-**: **white** precipitate of silver chloride, AgCl.
**Bromide, Br-**: **cream** precipitate of silver bromide, AgBr.
**Iodide, I-**: **yellow** precipitate of silver iodide, AgI.
Safety: silver nitrate stains skin and is an irritant, so wear eye protection and gloves.

callouts.p: The precipitates get darker down Group 7: white, cream, yellow (Cl, Br, I).

fig.cap: Figure 3: Halide test results after adding dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution: chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride, bromide a cream precipitate of silver bromide and iodide a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

core.h: Why add dilute nitric acid first?
core.p: As with the sulfate test, the acid is there to **remove carbonate ions**. Silver ions react with carbonate ions to form silver carbonate, a pale precipitate that could be confused with a silver halide. Nitric acid destroys the carbonate ions as carbon dioxide first.
bullets: Nitric acid removes CO3 2- ions: CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O.
**Do not use hydrochloric acid**: it contains chloride ions, which would give a white AgCl precipitate even if the sample had no chloride.
**Do not use sulfuric acid**: silver sulfate can also form a precipitate and confuse the result.
Nitrate ions do not form a precipitate with silver ions (all nitrates are soluble), so nitric acid adds nothing that interferes.
Spectator ions: in NaCl(aq) + AgNO3(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq), Na+ and NO3- do not change.

callouts.p: Sulfate test: hydrochloric acid with barium chloride. Halide test: nitric acid with silver nitrate. The acid never contains the ion you are testing for.

core.p: White, cream and yellow can look similar, especially in a small test tube or with dilute solutions. Grade 9 answers show awareness of this and suggest how to make the comparison reliable.
bullets: Compare the unknown precipitate with **known samples** of AgCl, AgBr and AgI made at the same time.
Look at the tubes side by side against a **white background**.
Use the **same volumes and concentrations** each time so the amount of precipitate is similar.
Silver halide precipitates darken in sunlight because they decompose, so observe them promptly (the reason they were used in photography).
A mixture of halides can give an in-between colour that is hard to interpret.

callouts.p: Edexcel mark schemes want white for chloride, cream for bromide, yellow for iodide. Do not write off-white or orange.

core.h: Writing ionic equations for anion tests
core.p: Each positive result is a reaction between the anion and one ion from the reagent. Write only those two (or three) species, balance atoms and charges, and include state symbols. The precipitate is **(s)** and the gas is **(g)**.
bullets: Carbonate: CO3 2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l)
Sulfate: Ba2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Chloride: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) → AgCl(s)
Bromide: Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) → AgBr(s)
Iodide: Ag+(aq) + I-(aq) → AgI(s)
The charges always cancel in a neutral precipitate: Ba2+ with SO4 2-, Ag+ with a halide ion (1-).

callouts.p: Silver nitrate is AgNO3 and silver ions are Ag+ (1+). Writing Ag2+ or AgNO2 loses the mark.

core.p: Use this as a checklist. In an unknown salt you can carry out all three tests on separate portions of the solution. Only one anion is usually present in a simple salt, so normally only one test is positive.
bullets: Always use **fresh portions** of the sample solution for each test, so reagents from one test do not affect another.
If the carbonate test is positive, the acidifying step in the other tests will cause fizzing too: this is expected.
Negative result: no fizzing, no precipitate, or limewater stays clear.
Record observations in a results table: test, observation, conclusion.

core.p: Exam questions often describe a flawed method and ask you to spot the problem. Most errors come from using the **wrong acid**, skipping the acid step, or contaminating the sample. Think about which ions each reagent adds to the tube.
bullets: **False positive**: a positive result when the ion is not actually there, for example HCl in the halide test giving white AgCl.
**Tap water** contains chloride and sometimes sulfate and carbonate ions, so always dissolve samples in **distilled (deionised) water**.
Clean apparatus between tests to avoid carry-over of ions.
Repeat a test or confirm with a second method if the result is unclear.
Chemical tests are quick and cheap, but rely on judging colours and work best on single, pure salts.

callouts.p: Say what is wrong (the reagent adds the ion being tested for) and what the effect is (a precipitate forms anyway, so the result is not valid).

analogy.t: Anion tests are like a lock and key, with a security guard first
analogy.p: Each reagent is a key that fits only one lock: barium ions lock onto sulfate, silver ions lock onto halides, and acid unlocks carbonate as a gas. The acid added first in the sulfate and halide tests is like a security guard who removes an impostor (carbonate ions) that would otherwise also open the lock and fool you. If you use the wrong guard, such as sulfuric acid or hydrochloric acid, you have smuggled in a key yourself and the lock opens no matter what. The analogy breaks down because real ions do not fit just one partner: silver ions form precipitates with all three halides, and you need the colour, not just whether it opens, to tell them apart.

terms.d: A negative ion, such as Cl-, SO4 2- or CO3 2-.
The ion CO3 2-, which reacts with acids to give carbon dioxide.
The ion SO4 2-, identified by a white precipitate with acidified barium chloride.
A negative ion of a Group 7 element: chloride Cl-, bromide Br- or iodide I-.
Fizzing caused by bubbles of gas being produced in a liquid.
Calcium hydroxide solution, which turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react.
BaSO4, the white insoluble precipitate that shows sulfate ions are present.
AgNO3, the reagent used to test for halide ions; its silver ions form silver halide precipitates.
An insoluble compound of silver and a halide: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream), AgI (yellow).
To add an acid to a solution, here to remove carbonate ions before a test.
A positive test result when the ion is not actually present in the sample.
An equation showing only the ions that react, with spectator ions left out.
An ion that is present in the mixture but does not take part in the reaction.
Water with dissolved ions removed, used so that the water does not affect the test.

mistakes.w: Carbonate test: add acid, it fizzes, so it is a carbonate.
mistakes.r: Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide.

mistakes.w: Sulfate test: add sulfuric acid then barium chloride.
mistakes.r: Add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution; sulfuric acid adds sulfate ions.

mistakes.w: Halide test: add hydrochloric acid then silver nitrate.
mistakes.r: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate; HCl adds chloride ions.

mistakes.w: The acid is added to make the reaction faster / to dissolve the salt.
mistakes.r: The acid removes carbonate ions, which would also form a precipitate.

mistakes.w: Bromide gives a yellow precipitate and iodide gives cream.
mistakes.r: Bromide gives cream (AgBr); iodide gives yellow (AgI).

mistakes.w: Sulfate gives a white precipitate of barium chloride.
mistakes.r: The white precipitate is barium sulfate, BaSO4.

mistakes.w: Limewater turns clear / turns white solid.
mistakes.r: Limewater turns milky (cloudy).

mistakes.w: Ag2+ + 2Cl- → AgCl2
mistakes.r: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) → AgCl(s)

mistakes.w: Barium sulfate dissolves in the acid.
mistakes.r: Barium sulfate is insoluble in dilute acid; barium carbonate would react, which is why the acid is used.

exam.q: Name the reagents used to test for sulfate ions.
model: Dilute hydrochloric acid.
Barium chloride solution.
exam.tip: Both reagents are needed for 2 marks.

exam.q: State the result of a positive test for iodide ions using acidified silver nitrate solution.
model: Yellow precipitate.
exam.tip: Say precipitate as well as the colour.

exam.q: Describe the test for carbonate ions, including the result.
model: Add dilute acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid).
Bubbles / effervescence seen; bubble gas through limewater.
Limewater turns milky (cloudy).
exam.tip: The limewater step carries a mark.

exam.q: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before silver nitrate in the halide test.
model: To react with / remove carbonate ions.
Carbonate ions would form a precipitate with silver ions (giving a false positive).
exam.tip: Answer both what it removes and why that matters.

exam.q: A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid and silver nitrate solution to a sample and gets a white precipitate. The student concludes the sample contains chloride ions. Explain why this conclusion is not valid.
model: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions.
So a white precipitate of silver chloride would form whether or not the sample contained chloride ions.
exam.tip: Evaluate by asking what each reagent adds.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction in a positive sulfate test.
model: Ba2+ + SO4 2- → BaSO4
exam.tip: Spectator ions (Na+, Cl-) are left out.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction between carbonate ions and hydrogen ions.
model: CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O
Correctly balanced.
exam.tip: Two H+ balance the 2- charge.

exam.q: Explain why limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
model: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide.
Forming insoluble calcium carbonate (a white precipitate).
exam.tip: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O.

exam.q: Three solutions contain sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide. Describe how you could identify each solution.
model: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution to a sample of each.
White precipitate: sodium chloride.
Cream precipitate: sodium bromide.
Yellow precipitate: sodium iodide.
exam.tip: Every colour must be matched to the right salt.

exam.q: A white solid is known to be one of sodium carbonate, sodium sulfate or sodium chloride. Plan a series of tests to identify the solid, explaining the results you would expect.
model: Dissolve the solid in distilled water and use separate portions for each test.
Add dilute hydrochloric acid to one portion: fizzing, and gas turning limewater milky, shows carbonate.
To a second portion add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution: white precipitate shows sulfate.
To a third portion add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution: white precipitate shows chloride.
The acids are added first to remove carbonate ions, which would otherwise form precipitates.
Only one test should be positive; that identifies the solid.
exam.tip: For 6 marks give reagents, observations and conclusions in a logical order, and justify the acid choices.

worked.q: A colourless solution gives no fizzing with dilute hydrochloric acid, and gives a white precipitate when barium chloride solution is then added. Identify the anion and write the ionic equation.
steps: No fizzing with acid, so no carbonate ions are present.
White precipitate with acidified barium chloride is barium sulfate.
So the anion is sulfate, SO4 2-.
Ba2+ is 2+ and SO4 2- is 2-, so they combine 1:1.
worked.ans: Sulfate ion, SO4 2-. Ba2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) → BaSO4(s).

worked.q: A student tests sodium carbonate solution with silver nitrate solution but forgets to add nitric acid first. A pale precipitate forms. The student says the solution contains chloride ions. Explain the error and how to correct it.
steps: Silver ions react with carbonate ions to form silver carbonate, a pale precipitate.
This is a false positive: the precipitate is not a silver halide.
Correct method: add dilute nitric acid first. It reacts with carbonate ions: CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O, so they are removed (fizzing seen).
Then add silver nitrate: no precipitate, as there are no halide ions.
worked.ans: The precipitate came from carbonate ions; acidifying with dilute nitric acid first removes them, and the test would then correctly show no halide.

worked.q: Suggest why a cream precipitate can be hard to identify, and how a student could make the halide test result more certain.
steps: Cream lies between white (AgCl) and yellow (AgI), so it is easy to misjudge.
Colour also depends on lighting and on how much precipitate forms.
Make known samples of AgCl, AgBr and AgI using known chloride, bromide and iodide solutions.
Compare the unknown side by side against a white background, using the same volumes and concentrations.
worked.ans: Compare with known silver halide precipitates made under the same conditions and viewed against a white background.

chem_edx.9.10.summary: Polymers are not only made in factories: living things make **natural polymers**, very long molecules built from many small monomers. For Edexcel you must recall three: **DNA** is a polymer made from **four different monomers called nucleotides**, **starch** is a polymer based on **sugars** (glucose), and **proteins** are polymers based on **amino acids**. Natural polymers form by **condensation polymerisation**, in which a small molecule (usually water) is released each time two monomers join, which links this point to the polyesters in 9.22C.

core.p: A **polymer** is a very large molecule made of many small repeating units called **monomers** joined by covalent bonds. **Natural polymers** are polymers made by living organisms. They are essential for life: they store information (DNA), store energy (starch) and build and run cells (proteins).
bullets: Synthetic polymers such as poly(ethene) are made by people, mostly from crude oil.
Natural polymers are made inside cells, catalysed by **enzymes**, at body temperature.
The three spec examples are **DNA**, **starch** (a carbohydrate) and **proteins**.
Each is made from a different type of monomer: **nucleotides**, **sugars** and **amino acids**.
All three are formed by **condensation polymerisation**.

callouts.p: DNA is a polymer made from four different monomers called nucleotides. Starch is a polymer based on sugars. Proteins are polymers based on amino acids.

core.h: Condensation polymerisation: how natural polymers form
core.p: In **condensation polymerisation** monomers with **two reactive groups** join together and a **small molecule, usually water, is lost** at each new bond. This is different from addition polymerisation, where alkene monomers join and nothing else is formed.
bullets: Each monomer must have **two functional groups** (one at each end) so the chain can keep growing in both directions.
Every time a bond forms between two monomers, **one molecule of water** is released.
So making a polymer from n monomers releases about n water molecules (strictly n - 1 for a single chain).
The reverse reaction, breaking the polymer back into monomers by adding water, is called **hydrolysis**; this is what happens when you digest food.
Polyesters (9.22C) are synthetic condensation polymers; DNA, starch and proteins are natural ones.

head: Feature
Addition polymerisation
Condensation polymerisation
rows: Alkenes with a C=C double bond

callouts.p: Monomers with two functional groups join to form a polymer, with the loss of a small molecule such as water each time a bond forms.

core.p: **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the polymer that stores the genetic instructions of every living organism. It is made from **four different monomers called nucleotides**.
bullets: Each **nucleotide** is made of three parts: a **phosphate group**, a **sugar** (deoxyribose) and a **base**.
There are **four different bases**: **A** (adenine), **T** (thymine), **C** (cytosine) and **G** (guanine), so there are four different nucleotides.
Nucleotides join phosphate to sugar to form a long **sugar-phosphate backbone**, with the bases sticking out.
DNA is made of **two strands** wound into a **double helix**.
The strands are held together by **hydrogen bonds** (weak forces) between pairs of bases: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G (**complementary base pairing**).
The **order (sequence) of bases** along the strand is the genetic code that tells cells which proteins to make.

callouts.p: DNA has four different monomers (nucleotides) because there are four different bases: A, T, C and G. Many synthetic polymers have only one type of monomer.
The monomer is the whole nucleotide (phosphate + sugar + base), not just the base.

core.p: Because DNA has four different monomers, the order they appear in can vary almost endlessly. A polymer made of only one monomer, like poly(ethene), cannot carry a message, but DNA can, just as a long string of four letters can spell out instructions.
bullets: A sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid in a protein.
Different sequences of bases code for different proteins.
Complementary base pairing allows DNA to be copied accurately when cells divide: each strand acts as a template.
DNA molecules are enormous: a single human chromosome contains one DNA molecule with millions of nucleotides.

core.p: **Carbohydrates** contain only **carbon, hydrogen and oxygen**. Simple sugars such as **glucose** (C6H12O6) are the monomers. Joining many glucose molecules gives the polymers **starch** and **cellulose** (and glycogen in animals).
bullets: **Starch** is a polymer based on sugars: it is made from many **glucose** monomers joined together.
Glucose molecules join by condensation polymerisation, with a **water molecule released** at each link.
Plants make glucose by photosynthesis and store it as starch, for example in potatoes, rice and wheat.
Starch is **insoluble**, so it is a good store: it does not dissolve and affect water movement in cells.
**Cellulose** is another glucose polymer that forms strong fibres in plant cell walls.
When we digest starch, enzymes (amylase) break it back down into sugars by **hydrolysis**.

callouts.p: A natural polymer based on sugars, made from many glucose monomers joined together.
Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present (from biology). Useful context but the chemistry spec point only requires you to recall what starch is made from.

core.h: Proteins: polymers based on amino acids
core.p: **Proteins** are polymers based on **amino acids**. About 20 different amino acids occur in living things, and they join in different orders to make thousands of different proteins.
bullets: Each amino acid has an **amine group** (-NH2) at one end and a **carboxylic acid group** (-COOH) at the other: two functional groups, as condensation polymerisation needs.
The -COOH group of one amino acid reacts with the -NH2 group of the next.
A **water molecule** is released each time and the new bond is called a **peptide link** (amide link), -CO-NH-.
A long chain of amino acids is called a **polypeptide**; one or more polypeptides fold to form a protein.
The **sequence of amino acids** decides how the chain folds and so what the protein does.
Examples: **enzymes** (biological catalysts), **haemoglobin**, **keratin** (hair and nails), **collagen**, antibodies and some hormones.

callouts.p: A natural polymer based on amino acids joined by condensation polymerisation.

callouts.t: Proteins are not made from sugars
callouts.p: Proteins contain nitrogen (from the amine group) as well as C, H and O. Carbohydrates contain only C, H and O.

core.p: The three natural polymers differ in their monomers, the number of different monomers and their function. Exam questions often ask you to match polymer to monomer.
bullets: **Starch**: one type of monomer (glucose), so it is a repeating chain with no information.
**Proteins**: about 20 types of monomer (amino acids), giving huge variety of shapes and jobs.
**DNA**: four types of monomer (nucleotides), enough to code information.
All three are made by condensation polymerisation, so water is released as they form.
All three can be broken down by hydrolysis, which uses water.

core.p: Comparing natural and synthetic polymers links this point to the problems with polymers in 9.23C.
bullets: Natural polymers are made in living cells using enzymes; most synthetic polymers are made from crude oil in industry.
Natural polymers are **biodegradable**: microorganisms have enzymes that can break them down.
Most synthetic addition polymers are **non-biodegradable** and persist in landfill.
Natural polymers usually have several different monomers; many synthetic addition polymers have just one.
Both are long-chain molecules held together by covalent bonds within the chain.

core.h: Breaking natural polymers down: hydrolysis and digestion
core.p: Because natural polymers form by losing water, they can be broken down by adding water back. This reaction is **hydrolysis**, and in the body it is catalysed by enzymes.
bullets: Starch + water gives glucose (catalysed by amylase).
Protein + water gives amino acids (catalysed by protease enzymes).
Digestion breaks large insoluble polymers into small soluble monomers that can be absorbed into the blood.
Your body then rebuilds the monomers into its own polymers, such as your own proteins.

callouts.p: Condensation: monomers join, water released. Hydrolysis: water added, polymer splits into monomers.

core.p: Top answers connect structure to function, using the idea that a polymer's properties depend on its monomers and how they are arranged.
bullets: DNA stores information because the **sequence** of its four nucleotides can vary.
Proteins have very varied jobs because 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order and fold into specific shapes.
Starch is a good energy store because it is a large, insoluble molecule built from glucose, which can be released when needed.
The release of water in condensation polymerisation is why the polymer's formula is not simply n times the monomer's formula.

core.p: Use these exact phrases; they are what mark schemes look for.
bullets: DNA is made from **four different monomers** called **nucleotides**
starch is a polymer **based on sugars** (glucose)
proteins are polymers **based on amino acids**
**condensation polymerisation**: **water** is released
**double helix**, **base pairs**, A-T and C-G
**peptide link** between amino acids

analogy.t: Natural polymers are like different kinds of beads on a string
analogy.p: Starch is a necklace made from identical white beads (glucose): long and useful, but it carries no pattern. Proteins are necklaces made from 20 colours of bead, so each necklace has its own pattern and folds into its own shape. DNA is a pair of necklaces using four colours of bead, where each bead on one string clips to a matching bead on the other (A with T, C with G). Every time you click two beads together a drop of water drips out (condensation). The analogy breaks down because real monomers are joined by covalent bonds formed in chemical reactions, the chains fold into three-dimensional shapes, and DNA's two strands are held by hydrogen bonds rather than clips.

terms.d: A very large molecule made from many small repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds.
A small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer.
A polymer made by living organisms, such as DNA, starch, cellulose and proteins.
Polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups join and a small molecule such as water is released at each link.
Breaking a molecule apart by reaction with water, for example digesting starch to glucose.
Deoxyribonucleic acid: a natural polymer made from four different monomers called nucleotides; it carries genetic information.
The monomer of DNA, made of a phosphate group, a sugar (deoxyribose) and one of four bases.
Part of a nucleotide: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G).
In DNA, A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, held by hydrogen bonds.
The shape of DNA: two strands twisted around each other.
A compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, such as sugars, starch and cellulose.
A simple sugar, C6H12O6, which is the monomer of starch and cellulose.
A natural polymer based on sugars (glucose), used as an energy store in plants.
The monomer of proteins; contains an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
A natural polymer based on amino acids joined by peptide links.
The -CO-NH- bond formed between two amino acids when water is released.

mistakes.w: DNA is made from four bases.
mistakes.r: DNA is a polymer made from four different monomers called nucleotides (each nucleotide contains one of four bases).

mistakes.w: Starch is made from amino acids.
mistakes.r: Starch is a polymer based on sugars (glucose); proteins are based on amino acids.

mistakes.w: Proteins are made of nucleotides.
mistakes.r: Proteins are polymers of amino acids; nucleotides are the monomers of DNA.

mistakes.w: Natural polymers form by addition polymerisation.
mistakes.r: They form by condensation polymerisation, releasing water at each link.

mistakes.w: Starch is a monomer.
mistakes.r: Starch is a polymer; glucose is the monomer.

mistakes.w: In DNA, A pairs with G.
mistakes.r: A pairs with T and C pairs with G (complementary base pairs).

mistakes.w: Condensation polymerisation gives only the polymer.
mistakes.r: A small molecule, usually water, is also produced each time two monomers join.

mistakes.w: DNA strands are held together by covalent bonds between bases.
mistakes.r: The two strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent bonds are within each strand.

exam.q: Name the monomers that make up DNA.
model: Nucleotides.
exam.tip: Not bases, not amino acids.

exam.q: How many different monomers are used to make DNA?
model: Four.
exam.tip: One for each base: A, T, C, G.

exam.q: State the type of monomer used to make proteins.
model: Amino acids.
exam.tip: Proteins = amino acids. Learn the pairs.

exam.q: Starch is a natural polymer. Name the type of molecule from which starch is made.
model: Sugar / glucose.
exam.tip: Either 'sugars' or 'glucose' is accepted.

exam.q: Draw lines to match each natural polymer to its monomer: DNA, protein, starch; amino acid, glucose, nucleotide.
model: DNA - nucleotide; protein - amino acid; starch - glucose (all three correct for 2 marks).
Any one correct for 1 mark.
exam.tip: A three-way match is usually worth 2 marks.

exam.q: Give two differences between the formation of poly(ethene) and the formation of starch.
model: Poly(ethene) forms by addition polymerisation; starch forms by condensation polymerisation.
Water is released when starch forms; no other product forms with poly(ethene) / poly(ethene) monomer is an alkene, starch monomer is glucose.
exam.tip: Write both sides of each difference.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
model: A polymer made of nucleotides.
Each nucleotide has a phosphate, a sugar and a base.
Two strands twisted into a double helix.
Bases pair A with T and C with G, held by hydrogen bonds.
exam.tip: Four separate facts for four marks.

exam.q: Explain why DNA can store genetic information but starch cannot.
model: DNA has four different monomers so their sequence/order can vary and code information.
Starch is made from only one monomer (glucose), so it has no varying sequence.
exam.tip: The key idea is sequence.

exam.q: Amino acids join to make proteins. Explain why this is called condensation polymerisation.
model: Many amino acid monomers join to form a long chain (polymer).
A small molecule, water, is released each time two amino acids join.
exam.tip: Name water.

exam.q: Compare DNA, starch and proteins as natural polymers. Refer to their monomers, how they are formed and their functions.
model: DNA is made from four different monomers called nucleotides.
Starch is made from glucose (a sugar) monomers.
Proteins are made from amino acids (about 20 different types).
All three form by condensation polymerisation, releasing water.
DNA stores genetic information in the sequence of bases.
Starch is an energy store in plants; proteins act as enzymes, structural materials (e.g. keratin) or carriers (haemoglobin).
All are biodegradable / broken down by hydrolysis, unlike most synthetic addition polymers.
exam.tip: Cover monomer, formation and function for each, then a similarity.

worked.q: Glucose has the formula C6H12O6. Explain why the formula of a section of starch made from 3 glucose units is not C18H36O18.
steps: Three glucose molecules have C18H36O18 in total.
Joining 3 monomers in a chain makes 2 links.
Each link releases one water molecule, H2O, so 2 H2O are lost.
Subtract: C18H36O18 - 2 H2O = C18H32O16.
worked.ans: Because starch forms by condensation polymerisation, water is lost at each link, so the chain is C18H32O16, not C18H36O18.

worked.q: A student says: 'Proteins, starch and DNA are all the same because they are all polymers.' Write a model answer evaluating this statement.
steps: Agree in part: all three are natural polymers made from many monomers joined by covalent bonds.
All three form by condensation polymerisation, releasing water, and are biodegradable.
But their monomers differ: proteins from amino acids, starch from glucose, DNA from four nucleotides.
Their functions differ: proteins are enzymes and structural molecules, starch stores energy, DNA stores genetic information.
Conclude.
worked.ans: The statement is only partly right: they share a polymer structure and condensation formation, but they differ in monomer, number of monomer types and function, so they are not the same.

chem_edx.9.11.summary: **Alcohols** are a **homologous series** of organic compounds whose **functional group is -OH** (the hydroxyl group). You must recall the formulae of the first four, **methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol C3H7OH and butan-1-ol C4H9OH**, and draw their displayed structures showing **every covalent bond**, including the O-H bond. Because they share the -OH group they react in similar ways, for example losing water in **dehydration** to form an alkene, while their physical properties change gradually as the carbon chain gets longer.

core.p: An **alcohol** is an organic compound containing the **-OH functional group** bonded to a carbon atom in a hydrocarbon chain. Alcohols contain only **carbon, hydrogen and oxygen**.
bullets: The **functional group** is the group of atoms that decides how a compound reacts. For alcohols it is **-OH**.
The -OH group is attached to a **saturated** carbon chain (all C-C bonds are single).
Alcohols are **not** hydrocarbons, because they contain oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen.
All alcohol names end in **-ol**.
The general formula of the alcohols is **CnH2n+1OH**.

callouts.p: An atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic reactions of a compound. The functional group of the alcohols is -OH.
The -OH in an alcohol is covalently bonded to carbon. Alcohols are not bases and do not contain hydroxide ions, OH-. Say hydroxyl group or -OH group, not hydroxide.

core.h: The four alcohols you must know
core.p: Learn the name, molecular formula and the way the formula is usually written (showing the -OH) for the first four members.
bullets: The prefix tells you the number of carbon atoms: **meth = 1, eth = 2, prop = 3, but = 4** (the same as alkanes).
Each formula is usually written with the **-OH at the end**, for example C2H5OH, so the functional group is clear.
The molecular formula can also be written in full, for example ethanol is C2H6O, but C2H5OH is preferred.
For propanol and butanol the spec only uses the isomers with -OH on the **end carbon**: propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol.
The **1** in propan-1-ol means the -OH is on carbon number 1 (the end of the chain).

callouts.p: Methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol C3H7OH, butan-1-ol C4H9OH.

core.p: A **displayed formula** shows every atom and **every covalent bond** as a line. Edexcel insists that all bonds are drawn, including the bond between O and H.
bullets: Each **carbon** atom forms **4** covalent bonds.
Each **hydrogen** atom forms **1** covalent bond.
Each **oxygen** atom forms **2** covalent bonds: one to carbon and one to hydrogen.
Draw the carbons in a straight chain joined by single bonds.
Put the -OH on the **end carbon** for propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol.
Write **C-O-H** with a bond line between O and H. Writing just OH at the end loses the mark when the question says show all covalent bonds.
Count up afterwards: hydrogens should total 2n + 2 (including the H on the oxygen).

callouts.p: After drawing, check every C has exactly four lines, every O has two and every H has one. Then count atoms against the molecular formula.
Students often attach the O to two carbons or forget the H on the oxygen. In an alcohol the O is bonded to one C and one H.

core.h: Displayed formulae of propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol
core.p: Propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol follow the same pattern: a chain of carbons, each carrying hydrogens, with the -OH on carbon 1. Each new member adds one more **-CH2-** unit to the chain.
bullets: Propan-1-ol: 3 carbons, 8 hydrogens (7 on carbon, 1 on oxygen), 1 oxygen.
Butan-1-ol: 4 carbons, 10 hydrogens (9 on carbon, 1 on oxygen), 1 oxygen.
The end carbon furthest from the -OH has 3 hydrogens; the middle carbons each have 2; the carbon bonded to O has 2.
In methanol the single carbon has 3 hydrogens plus the O.

core.p: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are members of a **homologous series**: a family of compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula.
bullets: Same **general formula**: CnH2n+1OH.
Same **functional group**: -OH.
Each member differs from the next by **CH2**.
Similar **chemical properties**, because the reactions are those of the -OH group.
A **gradual change (trend) in physical properties** such as boiling point as the chain gets longer.
Other homologous series include alkanes, alkenes and carboxylic acids (9.32C).

callouts.p: A series of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, in which each member differs from the next by CH2, with similar chemical properties and a gradual variation in physical properties.

core.p: As the carbon chain gets longer, the molecules get bigger and the **intermolecular forces** between them get stronger, so physical properties change gradually.
bullets: **Boiling point increases** with chain length, because more energy is needed to overcome the stronger intermolecular forces.
The first four alcohols are all **liquids** at room temperature.
**Solubility in water decreases** as the chain gets longer: methanol, ethanol and propanol mix completely with water; butanol is less soluble.
The -OH group makes the small alcohols soluble; the longer hydrocarbon part does not mix with water.
Alcohols are **volatile** and **flammable**.

callouts.p: Do not say covalent bonds break when alcohols boil. Boiling overcomes the weak forces between molecules, not the bonds inside them.

core.p: Because all members have the -OH group, they react in similar ways. Knowing one alcohol's reactions lets you predict the others'.
bullets: **Combustion**: alcohols burn in air to give carbon dioxide and water, for example C2H5OH + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 3H2O.
**Oxidation**: alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids, for example ethanol to ethanoic acid (9.31C).
**Dehydration**: alcohols can lose water to form alkenes (see next section).
Alcohols react with sodium to give hydrogen gas (more slowly than water does).
Ethanol is used as a fuel, a solvent and in alcoholic drinks; methanol is toxic.

core.p: **Dehydration** means removing water. When an alcohol is heated with a suitable catalyst, a molecule of **water** is removed and an **alkene** forms. The H and OH removed come from two neighbouring carbon atoms, and a **C=C double bond** forms between them.
bullets: Ethanol is dehydrated to **ethene**: C2H5OH gives C2H4 + H2O.
Typical conditions: passing ethanol vapour over a heated catalyst such as **aluminium oxide**, or heating with a concentrated acid catalyst such as phosphoric acid.
It is the reverse of making ethanol by **hydration** of ethene with steam.
Propan-1-ol is dehydrated to **propene**: C3H7OH gives C3H6 + H2O.
Butan-1-ol is dehydrated to butene: C4H9OH gives C4H8 + H2O.
Methanol cannot form an alkene this way because it has only one carbon atom, and a C=C bond needs two.
The alkene can be identified because it **decolourises bromine water** (orange to colourless), showing the product is unsaturated.

callouts.p: A reaction in which water is removed from a molecule. Dehydration of an alcohol produces an alkene and water.
CnH2n+1OH gives CnH2n + H2O.

core.p: Alkanes and alcohols with the same number of carbons look similar but have different properties because of the -OH group.
bullets: Ethane C2H6 is a hydrocarbon; ethanol C2H5OH contains oxygen.
Alkanes do not mix with water; short-chain alcohols do, because of the -OH group.
Alkanes are gases for C1 to C4; the first four alcohols are liquids.
Both are saturated (only single C-C bonds) and both burn to CO2 and H2O.

core.p: Because the alcohols form a homologous series, you can use the general formula **CnH2n+1OH** to work out the formula of any straight-chain alcohol.
bullets: Pentanol (5 carbons): C5H11OH.
Hexanol (6 carbons): C6H13OH.
Relative formula mass increases by 14 for each extra CH2 (C = 12, H = 1).
Mr of ethanol C2H5OH = (2 x 12) + (6 x 1) + 16 = 46.

core.p: These are the phrases mark schemes reward for this point.
bullets: functional group is **-OH** (hydroxyl)
**homologous series**, same **general formula** CnH2n+1OH
differ by **CH2**
**similar chemical properties**, **gradual change** in physical properties
**displayed formula** showing **all covalent bonds** including O-H
**dehydration**: water removed, **alkene** formed

analogy.t: Alcohols are like a family of trains with the same engine
analogy.p: Imagine a set of toy trains: every train has the same red engine at the front (the -OH group), and behind it a line of identical carriages (CH2 units). Methanol has one carriage, ethanol two, propanol three, butanol four. Because the engine is the same, they all behave alike: they go the same places (similar chemical reactions). But longer trains are heavier and harder to get moving (higher boiling points). In dehydration you uncouple the engine along with one small part of the last carriage, and the carriages link more tightly (a double bond forms). The analogy breaks down because a real -OH group is at the end of the chain bonded covalently to carbon, and the end carbon has three hydrogens rather than being identical to the others.

terms.d: An organic compound containing the -OH functional group attached to a carbon chain; general formula CnH2n+1OH.
The atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic reactions of a compound.
The -OH functional group of the alcohols, covalently bonded to carbon.
A family of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, each differing by CH2, with similar chemical properties.
A formula that fits every member of a homologous series; for alcohols CnH2n+1OH.
The alcohol with one carbon atom, CH3OH.
The alcohol with two carbon atoms, C2H5OH.
The alcohol with three carbon atoms and -OH on the end carbon, C3H7OH.
The alcohol with four carbon atoms and -OH on the end carbon, C4H9OH.
A drawing showing every atom in a molecule and every covalent bond as a line.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule, for example C2H6O for ethanol.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Removal of water from a molecule; an alcohol is dehydrated to an alkene and water.
A hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond, general formula CnH2n; formed by dehydrating an alcohol.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules; they increase with chain length, raising boiling point.

mistakes.w: The functional group of alcohols is OH- (hydroxide).
mistakes.r: The functional group is -OH, covalently bonded to carbon; alcohols are not alkalis.

mistakes.w: Ethanol is C2H6OH.
mistakes.r: Ethanol is C2H5OH (molecular formula C2H6O).

mistakes.w: Drawing O-H as just 'OH' at the end of a displayed formula.
mistakes.r: Show every covalent bond, including a line between O and H.

mistakes.w: Drawing the O between two carbons (C-O-C).
mistakes.r: In an alcohol the O is bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen: C-O-H.

mistakes.w: Alcohols are hydrocarbons.
mistakes.r: Alcohols contain oxygen, so they are not hydrocarbons.

mistakes.w: Members of a homologous series have the same physical properties.
mistakes.r: They have similar chemical properties and a gradual change (trend) in physical properties.

mistakes.w: Boiling point increases because covalent bonds get stronger.
mistakes.r: Boiling point increases because intermolecular forces get stronger as the molecules get bigger.

mistakes.w: Dehydration of ethanol gives ethane.
mistakes.r: Dehydration gives ethene (an alkene, C2H4) and water.

mistakes.w: Propanol has the -OH in the middle.
mistakes.r: Propan-1-ol has the -OH on carbon 1, the end of the chain.

exam.q: State the functional group present in all alcohols.
model: -OH (hydroxyl group).
exam.tip: Do not write OH- or hydroxide.

exam.q: Give the formula of propan-1-ol.
model: C3H7OH (accept CH3CH2CH2OH or C3H8O).
exam.tip: Writing the -OH at the end is safest.

exam.q: Draw the displayed formula of ethanol, showing all covalent bonds.
model: Two carbons joined by a single bond, with 5 H atoms correctly attached by single bonds.
-O-H attached to one carbon, with the O-H bond shown.
exam.tip: Check C has 4 bonds, O has 2, H has 1.

exam.q: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are in the same homologous series. Give two features of a homologous series.
model: Same general formula / same functional group.
Each member differs by CH2 / similar chemical properties / gradual change in physical properties.
exam.tip: Any two distinct features.

exam.q: What is the molecular formula of butan-1-ol?
model: C4H10O (accept C4H9OH).
exam.tip: Count all hydrogens, including the one on oxygen.

exam.q: Use the general formula to give the formula of the alcohol with 6 carbon atoms.
model: C6H13OH.
exam.tip: 2n + 1 = 13 hydrogens on carbon.

exam.q: Explain why the boiling point of butan-1-ol is higher than that of methanol.
model: Butan-1-ol molecules are larger / have a longer chain, so intermolecular forces are stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces.
exam.tip: Intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

exam.q: Ethanol can be dehydrated. Write a balanced equation for this reaction and name the organic product.
model: C2H5OH gives C2H4 + H2O.
Ethene.
exam.tip: Dehydration = water removed.

exam.q: Describe a test to show that the product of dehydrating propan-1-ol is an alkene.
model: Add (shake with) bromine water.
It changes from orange to colourless.
exam.tip: Colourless, not clear.

exam.q: Compare the structures and properties of ethane and ethanol. Use displayed formulae in your answer.
model: Ethane C2H6: two carbons each with three H, single C-C bond.
Ethanol C2H5OH: same carbon chain but one H replaced by -OH.
Ethanol displayed formula shows C-O-H with the O-H bond.
Both are saturated (only single bonds).
Ethane is a hydrocarbon/alkane; ethanol is an alcohol with the -OH functional group.
Ethanol is a liquid that mixes with water; ethane is a gas that does not mix with water.
Ethanol can be dehydrated to ethene / oxidised to ethanoic acid because of the -OH group; both burn to CO2 and H2O.
exam.tip: Cover structure (with drawings), physical properties and chemical properties.

worked.q: Draw the displayed formula of propan-1-ol and check it against its molecular formula.
steps: Draw three carbons in a row joined by single bonds: C-C-C.
Attach -O-H to the first carbon, showing the C-O and O-H bonds.
Fill each carbon to four bonds with hydrogens: end carbon 3 H, middle carbon 2 H, carbon 1 has 2 H plus the O.
Count: C = 3, H on carbon = 7, H on oxygen = 1, so H = 8, O = 1.
Molecular formula C3H8O, written as C3H7OH.
worked.ans: H3C-CH2-CH2-O-H with every bond drawn: C3H7OH (C3H8O). Every C has 4 bonds, O has 2, each H has 1.

worked.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of butan-1-ol and predict the formula of the alkene made when it is dehydrated. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Formula C4H9OH contains 4 C, 10 H and 1 O.
Dehydration removes H2O: C4H10O - H2O = C4H8.
C4H8 fits CnH2n so it is an alkene (butene).
worked.ans: Mr of butan-1-ol = 74. Dehydration gives butene, C4H8: C4H9OH gives C4H8 + H2O.

chem_edx.9.2.summary: In this core practical you identify both ions in an unknown salt by combining the cation tests (flame tests, sodium hydroxide and the ammonia test) with the anion tests (acid and limewater for carbonate, acidified barium chloride for sulfate, acidified silver nitrate for halides). You must plan a logical sequence of tests on separate portions of the sample, carry them out safely, record observations precisely and use them to deduce the name and formula of the salt. Exam questions test the method, the results, the reasons behind each step and how to spot invalid conclusions.

core.p: Edexcel core practical 9.6C asks you to **identify the ions in unknown salts**, using the tests for the specified cations and anions. Spec point 9.7C asks you to **identify the ions in unknown salts from the results of these tests**, which means exam questions often give you observations and ask you to work out the salt. Every simple salt has one cation and one anion, so you need at least one positive cation result and one positive anion result.
bullets: Cations you may need to find: **Li+, Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cu2+** (flame test) and **Al3+, Ca2+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, NH4+** (sodium hydroxide).
Anions you may need to find: **CO3 2-, SO4 2-, Cl-, Br-, I-**.
The final answer is the **name and formula** of the salt, for example copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4.
Using two tests that agree (e.g. a blue-green flame and a blue precipitate for Cu2+) makes the conclusion more certain.

callouts.p: A simple salt = one cation + one anion. Test for the cation and the anion separately, then combine them using their charges.

core.p: A good plan saves sample and avoids tests interfering with each other. Do the flame test on the **solid**, then dissolve some of the solid in **distilled water** and divide the solution into **separate portions**, using a fresh portion for each test. Never add the reagents for one test to a tube that has already had another test done in it.
bullets: Look first: the colour of the solid or solution is a clue (blue often means Cu2+, pale green Fe2+, yellow-brown Fe3+), but it is never proof on its own.
**Flame test** on a small amount of solid on a clean nichrome wire.
**Dissolve** about a spatula of solid in distilled water in a boiling tube.
Portion 1: add **sodium hydroxide solution** dropwise, then in excess (and warm with damp red litmus if no precipitate, to check for NH4+).
Portion 2: add **dilute acid** (carbonate test), bubbling any gas through limewater. This can also be done on the solid.
Portion 3: add **dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution** (sulfate test).
Portion 4: add **dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution** (halide test).

callouts.p: Reagents added in one test would contaminate the next. For example, the hydrochloric acid from the sulfate test adds chloride ions, which would then give a false white precipitate with silver nitrate.

fig.cap: Figure 1: A logical plan for identifying an unknown salt. The flame test is carried out on the solid; the solid is then dissolved in distilled water and separate portions are used for the sodium hydroxide test and the three anion tests.

core.p: A core practical answer should name the hazards and how to reduce the risk. You are expected to wear **eye protection** throughout, and to know which reagents need extra care.
bullets: **Concentrated hydrochloric acid** (cleaning the flame test wire) is **corrosive**: use small amounts, wear eye protection, avoid skin contact.
**Sodium hydroxide solution** is corrosive or irritant: wear eye protection; wash any splashes off skin with plenty of water.
**Barium chloride solution** is **toxic**: avoid contact and wash hands after use.
**Silver nitrate solution** is an irritant and **stains skin**: wear gloves and eye protection.
**Bunsen burner**: tie hair back, keep the area clear, use a heat-proof mat.
**Ammonia gas** is irritating: warm gently, do not boil, ensure good ventilation and never sniff directly.
Some unknown salts may themselves be harmful (e.g. copper and barium salts), so use small amounts.

callouts.p: When warming with NaOH for the ammonium test, heat gently and point the tube away from people: boiling alkali can spit out of the tube.

core.p: Start with the flame test, because it uses solid and quickly narrows the options. Then use sodium hydroxide on the solution: it can confirm the flame result and identifies ions that have no useful flame colour, such as Al3+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and NH4+.
bullets: Clean a nichrome wire loop in concentrated HCl and a blue flame until it gives **no colour**.
Dip the wire in the solid and hold it in the **edge of a blue Bunsen flame**; record the colour.
Flame colours: Li+ **red (crimson)**, Na+ **yellow**, K+ **lilac**, Ca2+ **orange-red**, Cu2+ **blue-green**.
Add NaOH(aq) **dropwise** to about 1 cm3 of solution; record the precipitate colour.
Precipitates: Al3+ **white, dissolves in excess**; Ca2+ **white, stays in excess**; Cu2+ **blue**; Fe2+ **green**; Fe3+ **brown**.
If there is no precipitate, **warm gently** and hold **damp red litmus** at the mouth of the tube: turning blue shows **ammonia**, so NH4+ is present.
No precipitate and no ammonia means the cation is probably Li+, Na+ or K+, which the flame test identifies.

callouts.p: If a flame test gives an unexpected or mixed colour, the sample may contain more than one metal ion; a strong colour such as sodium's yellow can mask another.

fig.cap: Figure 2: Decision tree for the sodium hydroxide test. The colour of the precipitate identifies Cu2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+; a white precipitate is tested with excess NaOH to separate Al3+ from Ca2+; no precipitate leads to warming with damp red litmus (NH4+) or to the flame test (Group 1 ions).
