core.p: If the **oxygen supply is limited**, there is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon to CO2. The hydrogen is still oxidised to water, but some carbon ends up as **carbon monoxide (CO)** or as solid **carbon (soot)**.
bullets: Methane making carbon monoxide: **2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O**
Methane making soot: **CH4 + O2 → C + 2H2O**
Ethene making carbon monoxide: **C2H4 + 2O2 → 2CO + 2H2O**
Ethene making soot: **C2H4 + O2 → 2C + 2H2O**
Incomplete combustion releases **less energy** per mole of fuel than complete combustion.
It gives a **yellow, smoky flame** (Bunsen burner with the air hole closed).

head: Feature
Complete combustion
Incomplete combustion
rows: Carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot), some CO2

callouts.p: Students often forget that water is a product of incomplete combustion too. Only the carbon product changes.

core.h: Why carbon monoxide and soot are harmful
core.p: The products of incomplete combustion cause health and environmental problems, which is why appliances need a good air supply and regular servicing.
bullets: Carbon monoxide is **toxic**: it **combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells**, reducing the blood's ability to **carry oxygen**.
CO is **colourless and odourless**, so it cannot be detected by our senses; a CO detector is needed.
Soot (carbon particulates) can cause **breathing problems** and lung disease.
Soot makes buildings dirty and can cause **global dimming** by reflecting sunlight.
Incomplete combustion also wastes fuel because less energy is released.

callouts.p: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, so less oxygen can be carried in the blood.

core.h: Alkanes versus alkenes: the smoky flame
core.p: Alkenes burn with a **smokier, more yellow flame** than alkanes with the same number of carbon atoms. This is because alkenes have a **higher proportion of carbon** (and lower proportion of hydrogen), so in air there is often not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon, and more **incomplete combustion** occurs.
bullets: Ethane C2H6: C:H ratio 1:3, about **80% carbon by mass**.
Ethene C2H4: C:H ratio 1:2, about **86% carbon by mass**.
More carbon per molecule needs more oxygen, so unburnt carbon forms **soot**.
Both still give only CO2 and H2O if oxygen is in excess.
This smoky flame is one reason alkenes are **not used as fuels**; they are more valuable for making **polymers** and other chemicals.

callouts.p: For full marks: alkene has a higher percentage of carbon, so needs more oxygen, so incomplete combustion is more likely, producing soot (carbon) which gives the smoky flame.

fig.cap: An alkane such as ethane burns with a cleaner flame and makes carbon dioxide and water. An alkene such as ethene burns with a smoky yellow flame because some of its carbon is released unburnt as soot.

core.h: Calculating percentage of carbon by mass
core.p: You can show that alkenes contain more carbon using relative formula mass (Mr). Use Ar: C = 12, H = 1.
bullets: % carbon = (total mass of carbon atoms ÷ Mr) × 100
Every alkene has the same % carbon (85.7%) because the C:H ratio is always 1:2.
For alkanes the % carbon rises as the chain gets longer but never reaches 85.7%.

core.h: Combustion as oxidation: the link to other topics
core.p: Combustion fits into wider ideas in the course. The carbon dioxide made adds to the greenhouse effect, and burning fuels is the main use of alkanes from crude oil.
bullets: Alkanes from crude oil (petrol, diesel, kerosene, natural gas) are burned as **fuels**.
Combustion releases **carbon dioxide**, a **greenhouse gas** linked to climate change.
Fuels containing sulfur impurities also give **sulfur dioxide**, which causes **acid rain** (not a product of the pure hydrocarbon).
High temperatures in engines make nitrogen and oxygen in air react to form **oxides of nitrogen**.
Alcohols also burn completely to give CO2 and H2O (studied later in this topic).

callouts.p: A pure hydrocarbon contains no sulfur, so it cannot make SO2. SO2 only comes from sulfur impurities in the fuel.

analogy.p: Think of a hydrocarbon molecule as a Lego model built from black carbon bricks and white hydrogen bricks. Burning it is like taking the model apart and clipping every brick onto red oxygen bricks: each black brick gets two red bricks (CO2) and each pair of white bricks gets one red brick (H2O). If you run out of red bricks (limited oxygen), some black bricks only get one red brick (CO) or none at all (soot). An alkene model has more black bricks for its size, so you are more likely to run short. The analogy breaks down because Lego bricks are not changed and no energy is released, whereas real bond breaking and making transfers energy and the products are completely new substances.

terms.d: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single C-C bonds, general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond, general formula CnH2n.
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy as heat and light.
Combustion in a plentiful supply of oxygen; a hydrocarbon forms only carbon dioxide and water.
Combustion in a limited supply of oxygen; forms water plus carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot).
The gain of oxygen by a substance (or loss of electrons).
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A substance that releases useful energy when it is burned.
A toxic, colourless, odourless gas (CO) that combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen the blood can carry.
Solid particles of carbon produced by incomplete combustion.
Calcium hydroxide solution; turns milky (cloudy) when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
A white solid that turns blue when water is added; used to test for water.
A symbol equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that absorbs infrared radiation and keeps the Earth warm.
Reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth's surface caused by particulates such as soot.

mistakes.w: Hydrocarbons burn to make carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
mistakes.r: The hydrogen is oxidised to water, so the products are carbon dioxide and water.

mistakes.w: Combustion is a reduction reaction.
mistakes.r: Combustion is oxidation: the hydrocarbon gains oxygen.

mistakes.w: Complete combustion happens in a limited amount of air.
mistakes.r: Complete combustion needs a plentiful or excess supply of oxygen.

mistakes.w: Incomplete combustion does not produce water.
mistakes.r: Water is still formed; only the carbon product changes to CO and/or C.

mistakes.w: Alkenes burn with a smoky flame because they have a double bond.
mistakes.r: Alkenes have a higher percentage of carbon, so incomplete combustion is more likely, producing soot.

mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is a greenhouse gas.
mistakes.r: CO is toxic because it combines with haemoglobin, reducing the oxygen carried by the blood.

mistakes.w: Limewater goes clear / goes blue with carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Limewater turns milky or cloudy.

mistakes.w: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O
mistakes.r: Balanced: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O.

mistakes.w: Burning methane produces sulfur dioxide.
mistakes.r: Pure hydrocarbons contain no sulfur; SO2 only forms from sulfur impurities in fuels.

exam.q: Name the two products of the complete combustion of propene.
model: carbon dioxide
water
exam.tip: The same two products form for any alkane or alkene burning completely.

exam.q: Explain why the complete combustion of an alkane is described as an oxidation reaction.
model: the alkane/carbon and hydrogen gain oxygen
to form carbon dioxide and water
exam.tip: Use the definition of oxidation and link it to both products.

exam.q: Balance the equation: C3H8 + ...O2 → ...CO2 + ...H2O
exam.tip: Balance C, then H, then O last.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethene, C2H4.
model: correct formulae of products CO2 and H2O
exam.tip: One mark is often for formulae, one for balancing.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane, C4H10.
model: correct formulae: C4H10 + O2 → CO2 + H2O
2C4H10 + 13O2 → 8CO2 + 10H2O (accept C4H10 + 6½O2 → 4CO2 + 5H2O)
exam.tip: If you get a half, double everything; both forms are usually accepted.

exam.q: Describe a test to show that water is produced when a hydrocarbon burns.
model: add (anhydrous) copper(II) sulfate / collect liquid in cooled U-tube and add copper sulfate
turns from white to blue
exam.tip: Both the starting and final colour are needed for the mark.

exam.q: State the conditions needed for complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
model: a plentiful / excess supply of oxygen (or air)
exam.tip: 'Oxygen' alone is not enough; say plentiful or excess.

exam.q: Ethane and ethene both burn in air. Ethene burns with a much smokier flame. Explain why.
model: ethene has a higher proportion/percentage of carbon (lower proportion of hydrogen)
so more incomplete combustion occurs / not enough oxygen to burn all the carbon
producing (unburnt) carbon / soot
exam.tip: Build a chain of reasoning: composition → oxygen → incomplete combustion → soot.

exam.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous to humans.
model: it combines with haemoglobin (in red blood cells)
reducing the amount of oxygen the blood can carry
exam.tip: Mention that it is colourless and odourless only if a third mark is available.

exam.q: Calculate the percentage by mass of carbon in ethene, C2H4. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
model: Mr = 28
exam.tip: Show the Mr first; it earns a mark even if the final answer is wrong.

exam.q: A student burns a hydrocarbon in a limited supply of air. Compare the products and the energy released with burning it in excess oxygen. [6 marks]
model: in excess oxygen, complete combustion occurs
products are carbon dioxide and water only
the hydrocarbon is fully oxidised and maximum energy is released
in limited air, incomplete combustion occurs
products include carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water (some CO2)
less energy is released; yellow smoky flame; CO is toxic as it binds to haemoglobin
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need comparison: use 'whereas' and cover products, energy and hazards.

worked.q: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of pentane, C5H12.
steps: Write the unbalanced equation: C5H12 + O2 → CO2 + H2O
Balance carbon: 5 C atoms so 5CO2
Balance hydrogen: 12 H atoms so 6H2O
Count oxygen on the right: (5 × 2) + (6 × 1) = 16 O atoms, so 8O2

worked.q: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 22 g of propane, C3H8, burns completely. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Equation: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O
Moles of propane = 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol
Ratio propane : CO2 = 1 : 3, so moles CO2 = 1.5 mol
Mass of CO2 = 1.5 × 44 = 66 g
worked.ans: 66 g of carbon dioxide

worked.q: Explain, using percentages by mass, why propene (C3H6) gives a smokier flame than propane (C3H8).
steps: Propene has a higher percentage of carbon
So more oxygen is needed per gram to oxidise all the carbon, and in air incomplete combustion is more likely
Unburnt carbon is released as soot, making the flame smoky and yellow
worked.ans: Propene is 85.7% carbon compared with 81.8% for propane, so it undergoes more incomplete combustion and produces more soot.

chem_edx.9.7.summary: A **polymer** is a substance of **high average relative molecular mass** made up of **small repeating units**. **Addition polymers** form when many small **monomer** molecules containing a **C=C double bond** join together: the double bond opens up and the monomers link into a long saturated chain, with **no other product**. Poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) (PVC) and PTFE are made this way, and each is used for jobs that match its properties, so you must be able to draw the polymer from the monomer, work backwards from the polymer to the monomer, and explain each use.

core.p: Polymers are very large molecules (macromolecules) built by joining thousands of small molecules called **monomers**. The chains in a sample are not all the same length, which is why we talk about an **average** relative molecular mass.
bullets: **Monomer**: a small molecule that can join with others to make a polymer.
**Polymer**: a long-chain molecule made of many repeating units.
**Polymerisation**: the reaction that joins monomers together.
Each chain may contain thousands of monomer units, so Mr is very high (often tens of thousands or more).
Chains have different lengths, so a polymer sample has an **average** Mr rather than one exact value.
Plastics are synthetic polymers; DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose are natural polymers.

callouts.p: A polymer is a substance of high average relative molecular mass made up of small repeating units.

core.p: In **addition polymerisation**, monomers that contain a **carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)** join together. One of the two bonds in each C=C **breaks (opens up)** and the electrons are used to form new single C-C bonds to neighbouring monomers.
bullets: Monomers must be **unsaturated**: they contain a C=C double bond (alkenes or alkene-like molecules).
The polymer is **saturated**: its backbone has only single C-C bonds.
The polymer is the **only product**; no small molecule is given off.
Because nothing is lost, the **repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer** (same molecular formula).
Mass of polymer formed = total mass of monomer used (atom economy 100%).
The reaction usually needs **high pressure** and a **catalyst** (details vary for each polymer).

callouts.p: Polymer name = poly + (monomer name in brackets): ethene gives poly(ethene).
Poly(ethene) does NOT decolourise bromine water because it has no C=C double bonds left.

core.p: **Ethene** (C2H4) molecules join together to make **poly(ethene)**, often called polythene. Each ethene molecule's C=C opens, and the carbon atoms link to form a very long chain of CH2 groups.
bullets: Equation: **n CH2=CH2 → -(CH2-CH2)n-**
**n** is a large number: the number of monomer molecules joined.
The repeating unit is **-CH2-CH2-** drawn inside brackets with bonds going **through** the brackets.
Poly(ethene) is a saturated hydrocarbon, like a very long alkane.
The formula of the repeating unit (C2H4) equals the monomer formula.

callouts.p: Marks are given for: single C-C bond between the two carbons, extension bonds through both brackets, all side atoms correct, and n after the bracket.

core.h: How to draw a repeating unit from a monomer
core.p: Every addition polymer can be drawn from its monomer using the same four steps. The only thing that changes from one polymer to another is which atoms or groups are attached to the two carbons.
bullets: Step 1: draw the two C=C carbons from the monomer **side by side**.
Step 2: change the **double bond to a single bond**.
Step 3: keep every other atom or group (H, CH3, Cl, F) **in the same position** above and below the carbons.
Step 4: draw a bond out from each carbon **through square or round brackets**, and write **n** after the closing bracket.
Groups attached to the C=C end up as **side groups** hanging off the chain; they are not part of the backbone.
To show a longer section, repeat the unit several times joined by single bonds.

callouts.p: Do not leave the double bond in the repeating unit, and do not put the CH3 group into the main chain of poly(propene).

core.p: **Propene** (C3H6) has the structure CH2=CH-CH3. Only the two carbons of the C=C go into the backbone; the **CH3 group becomes a side group** on every other carbon of the chain.
bullets: Equation: **n CH2=CHCH3 → -(CH2-CH(CH3))n-**
The backbone is still a chain of single C-C bonds.
The CH3 side groups stick out from the chain.
Repeating unit formula C3H6, the same as propene.

core.p: **Chloroethene** (old name vinyl chloride) is CH2=CHCl: ethene with one H replaced by a **chlorine atom**. Its polymer is **poly(chloroethene)**, better known as **PVC**.
bullets: Equation: **n CH2=CHCl → -(CH2-CHCl)n-**
Each repeating unit carries one Cl atom as a side group.
PVC is not a hydrocarbon because it contains chlorine.
Rigid PVC (uPVC) is used for window frames and pipes; adding **plasticisers** makes it flexible for cable insulation.

callouts.p: Chloroethene → poly(chloroethene) = PVC. Both names may appear in the exam.

core.p: **Tetrafluoroethene** is CF2=CF2: ethene with **all four** hydrogen atoms replaced by **fluorine**. It polymerises to **poly(tetrafluoroethene)**, PTFE (trade name Teflon).
bullets: Equation: **n CF2=CF2 → -(CF2-CF2)n-**
'Tetra' means four: four fluorine atoms per monomer.
The C-F bonds are **very strong**, so PTFE is extremely **unreactive** and has a high melting point.
The fluorine atoms make the surface **very slippery (low friction)** and **non-stick**.

core.h: Deducing the polymer from a monomer
core.p: Exams often give an unfamiliar monomer, such as CH2=CHCN or CH2=CHC6H5 (styrene), and ask for the polymer. Use the same four steps: the method works for any monomer with a C=C.
bullets: Find the **C=C**: only those two carbons go into the backbone.
Everything else attached to those two carbons becomes side groups in the same positions.
Replace the C=C with C-C, add extension bonds through brackets and add n.
Example: CH2=CHCN gives **-(CH2-CH(CN))n-**, poly(propenenitrile).
Example: styrene CH2=CHC6H5 gives **-(CH2-CH(C6H5))n-**, poly(styrene).

callouts.p: Count the atoms: the repeating unit must contain exactly the same atoms as the monomer.

core.h: Deducing the monomer from a polymer
core.p: Working backwards is the reverse process. Find the **repeating unit**, which in an addition polymer is always **two carbons long** in the backbone, then put the double bond back.
bullets: Step 1: identify the two backbone carbons in the repeating unit (the bracketed section).
Step 2: **remove the extension bonds and brackets** and the n.
Step 3: change the C-C between the two carbons into **C=C**.
Step 4: keep all side atoms and groups where they were.
Example: -(CH2-CHCl)n- comes from **CH2=CHCl, chloroethene**.
If you are shown a long chain, look for the pattern of side groups that repeats every two carbons.

callouts.p: In a chain section like -CH2-CHCl-CH2-CHCl-, the repeating unit is CH2-CHCl, not the whole four carbons.

core.p: The use of each polymer is chosen because of its properties. Learn at least two uses and the property that explains each.
bullets: All four are **unreactive**, so they do not corrode or rot and are safe for food and water.
All four are **electrical insulators**.
All four are **lightweight** compared with metals or glass.
Being unreactive also means they are **non-biodegradable**, causing disposal problems (covered in 9.23C).

head: Polymer
Monomer
Properties
Uses
rows: Flexible, cheap, waterproof, light, electrical insulator
Plastic bags, cling film, squeezy bottles, cable insulation
Strong, tough, flexible, can withstand heating, hard-wearing
Crates, ropes, food containers, carpets, kettles

core.p: An 'explain' question needs a **property and the reason that property suits the use**. Just naming the property is usually worth only one mark.
bullets: Poly(ethene) for **carrier bags**: flexible and strong enough to hold shopping, waterproof and cheap to make.
Poly(propene) for **ropes and crates**: strong and tough so it does not snap or crack under load, and flexible.
Poly(propene) for **food containers**: withstands higher temperatures (e.g. dishwasher, hot food) than poly(ethene).
PVC for **window frames and pipes**: rigid and tough, does not rot or corrode, so it lasts outdoors without painting.
PVC for **cable insulation**: electrical insulator, and flexible when plasticised.
PTFE for **frying pans**: non-stick and slippery so food does not stick, unreactive and high melting point so it is not damaged by heat.
PTFE for **waterproof clothing**: water-repellent, so rain cannot soak through.

callouts.p: Use 'because' in every sentence: 'PVC is used for gutters because it is unreactive so does not corrode in rain.'

core.h: Key facts to compare with condensation polymers
core.p: Addition polymerisation will be compared with condensation polymerisation (polyesters, 9.22C), so be clear about its features.
bullets: Monomers: one type of monomer with a **C=C double bond**.
Products: **only the polymer**, no water or other small molecule.
Empirical formula of polymer = empirical formula of monomer.
Backbone: carbon atoms only, joined by single bonds.
Polymer chains are held together by intermolecular forces; longer chains give stronger forces and higher melting points.

callouts.p: Addition polymer: many unsaturated monomers join, the C=C opens, one product only.

analogy.p: Imagine each monomer is a paper strip already folded into a closed loop with a clip (the C=C double bond). To make a chain, you unclip one side of each loop and hook it onto the next strip, so the clips that held each loop closed now hold neighbouring strips together. Thousands of strips give one long paper chain (the polymer) and nothing is left over, just as no other product forms in addition polymerisation. Coloured stickers on each strip (H, CH3, Cl or F) stay attached and hang off the chain as side groups. The analogy breaks down because real chains are not all the same length, the chains are tangled in three dimensions, and the 'unclipping' is a chemical change involving electrons, not a physical one.

terms.d: A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
A substance of high average relative molecular mass made up of small repeating units.
A reaction in which many monomer molecules join to form a polymer.
Polymerisation in which unsaturated monomers with a C=C double bond join together to form a polymer as the only product.
The section of a polymer that is repeated along the chain; drawn in brackets with n.
Contains at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
Contains only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Addition polymer made from ethene; flexible, cheap, used for bags and bottles.
Addition polymer made from propene; strong and tough, used for crates and ropes.
Addition polymer made from chloroethene; tough and durable, used for window frames, pipes and cable insulation.
Poly(tetrafluoroethene), made from tetrafluoroethene; very unreactive and non-stick, used for coating frying pans.
Monomer CH2=CHCl used to make PVC.
Monomer CF2=CF2 used to make PTFE.
An atom or group attached to the polymer backbone, such as CH3 in poly(propene) or Cl in PVC.
A substance added to a polymer such as PVC to make it softer and more flexible.
The mean Mr of the polymer chains in a sample; used because the chains have different lengths.

mistakes.w: Draws the repeating unit of poly(ethene) with a C=C double bond.
mistakes.r: The double bond opens: the repeating unit has a single C-C bond.

mistakes.w: Draws brackets without bonds passing through them, or leaves out n.
mistakes.r: Extension bonds must go through both brackets and n is written after the closing bracket.

mistakes.w: Puts the CH3 group of poly(propene) into the main chain.
mistakes.r: Only the two C=C carbons are in the backbone; CH3 is a side group.

mistakes.w: Addition polymerisation produces a polymer and water.
mistakes.r: Addition polymerisation forms the polymer only; water is a product of condensation polymerisation.

mistakes.w: A polymer is a very big molecule (no mention of repeating units).
mistakes.r: A substance of high average relative molecular mass made up of small repeating units.

mistakes.w: PTFE is used in frying pans because it is strong.
mistakes.r: PTFE is non-stick/slippery, and unreactive with a high melting point so it survives heating.

mistakes.w: PVC is used for windows because it is cheap.
mistakes.r: PVC is tough and durable, and unreactive so it does not rot or corrode.

mistakes.w: Gives the monomer of PVC as chlorethane or CH2Cl-CH3.
mistakes.r: The monomer is chloroethene, CH2=CHCl, which must have a C=C double bond.

mistakes.w: Poly(ethene) decolourises bromine water because it came from ethene.
mistakes.r: Poly(ethene) is saturated, so bromine water stays orange.

exam.q: State what is meant by a polymer.
model: a substance of high average relative molecular mass
made up of small repeating units
exam.tip: Learn the spec definition word for word.

exam.q: Name the polymer formed from propene.
model: poly(propene)
exam.tip: Accept polypropene or polypropylene.

exam.q: Draw the repeating unit of poly(ethene).
model: two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, each with two H atoms
extension bonds through brackets and n
exam.tip: Check you have no double bond left.

exam.q: Draw the structure of the polymer formed from chloroethene, CH2=CHCl, showing one repeating unit.
model: backbone of two C atoms with single bond; three H and one Cl correctly placed
extension bonds through brackets and n
exam.tip: Keep the Cl on the same carbon as in the monomer.

exam.q: The repeating unit of a polymer is -(CF2-CF2)n-. Draw the displayed formula of its monomer and name it.
model: CF2=CF2 drawn with a C=C double bond and four F atoms
tetrafluoroethene
exam.tip: Remove brackets and n, then restore the double bond.

exam.q: Explain why ethene can be used to make an addition polymer but ethane cannot.
model: ethene is unsaturated / has a C=C double bond
ethane is saturated / has only single bonds so cannot open up to join
exam.tip: Mention both molecules for both marks.

exam.q: State why the mass of poly(ethene) formed is equal to the mass of ethene used.
model: no other product is formed / all atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer
exam.tip: Link to atom economy if asked: it is 100%.

exam.q: Explain why PVC is used for window frames.
model: it is tough / rigid / durable
it is unreactive so does not rot or corrode (needs no painting)
exam.tip: Give the property AND why that property matters for the use.

exam.q: Explain why PTFE is used to coat frying pans.
model: non-stick / slippery / low friction so food does not stick
unreactive / high melting point so it is not damaged when heated
exam.tip: Two different properties earn two marks.

exam.q: Compare the properties of poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC and PTFE and explain how these make each polymer suitable for its uses. [6 marks]
model: poly(ethene) is flexible, cheap and waterproof so is used for plastic bags and bottles
poly(propene) is strong and tough (and withstands heat) so is used for crates, ropes and food containers
PVC is tough and durable and does not rot or corrode so is used for window frames, gutters and pipes
PVC is an electrical insulator (flexible with plasticiser) so is used for cable insulation
PTFE is non-stick/slippery and very unreactive with a high melting point so is used for frying pans
all are unreactive, light and insulators; PTFE is also waterproof so used in waterproof clothing
exam.tip: Cover all four polymers with a property and a matching use for each; a balanced answer scores in the top band.

worked.q: The monomer styrene has the formula CH2=CH(C6H5), where C6H5 is a ring of carbon atoms. Describe how to draw the repeating unit of poly(styrene).
steps: Identify the C=C: it is between the CH2 carbon and the CH carbon.
Draw these two carbons side by side with a single bond between them.
Put two H atoms on the first carbon; on the second carbon put one H and the C6H5 group.
Draw a bond out of each end through brackets.
Write n after the closing bracket.
worked.ans: -(CH2-CH(C6H5))n-, with the C6H5 ring as a side group; the ring is not part of the backbone.

worked.q: A section of polymer chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-. Identify the repeating unit and name the monomer.
steps: Look for the pattern that repeats: CH2 then CH(CH3).
So the repeating unit is two carbons: -(CH2-CH(CH3))-.
Remove the extension bonds and turn the C-C into C=C: CH2=CH(CH3).
This molecule has three carbons and one double bond: propene.
worked.ans: Repeating unit -(CH2-CH(CH3))n-; monomer propene, CH2=CHCH3.

worked.q: A sample of poly(chloroethene) has an average relative molecular mass of 62 500. Estimate the average number of monomer units in each chain. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
steps: Monomer CH2=CHCl, formula C2H3Cl.
Because addition polymerisation loses nothing, Mr of repeating unit = 62.5
Number of units n = 62 500 ÷ 62.5 = 1000
worked.ans: About 1000 monomer units per chain (an average, because chains vary in length).

chem_edx.9.8.summary: Polyesters are made by **condensation polymerisation**, in which monomers that each have **two functional groups** react together and a **small molecule, water, is eliminated** every time a link forms. A **dicarboxylic acid** (two -COOH groups) reacts with a **diol** (two -OH groups), and each -COOH joins to an -OH to form an **ester link (-COO-)**, so the monomers alternate along the chain. Unlike addition polymerisation, there are **two products**: the polyester and water.

core.p: In **condensation polymerisation**, monomers join together and **a small molecule is lost** each time a bond forms between them. For polyesters the small molecule is **water**.
bullets: Each monomer must have **two functional groups**, one at each end, so it can join on both sides and build a chain.
Usually there are **two different monomers** that alternate along the chain.
There are **two products**: the polymer and a small molecule (water for polyesters).
Because water is removed, the repeating unit has **fewer atoms** than the two monomers added together.
'Condensation' = joining with loss of water (or another small molecule).

callouts.p: A reaction in which monomers with two functional groups join together to form a polymer, with the elimination of a small molecule such as water.

core.h: The two monomers for a polyester
core.p: A polyester is made from a **dicarboxylic acid** and a **diol**. The prefix 'di' tells you each molecule has **two** of that functional group, one at each end.
bullets: **Dicarboxylic acid**: two carboxyl groups, **-COOH**, e.g. HOOC-CH2-COOH or HOOC-COOH.
**Diol**: two hydroxyl (alcohol) groups, **-OH**, e.g. ethane-1,2-diol HO-CH2-CH2-OH.
The -COOH group is the functional group of carboxylic acids; -OH is the functional group of alcohols.
In exams the middle of each molecule is often drawn as a **box (block)** because only the end groups react.
A molecule with only one functional group would stop the chain growing, because it can only join on one side.

callouts.p: Polyester = dicarboxylic acid + diol, with water eliminated.

fig.cap: The two kinds of monomer drawn as block diagrams. The dicarboxylic acid has a carboxyl group at each end and the diol has a hydroxyl group at each end; the blocks stand for the rest of each molecule, which does not react.

core.p: A **carboxyl group (-COOH)** on the acid reacts with a **hydroxyl group (-OH)** on the diol. The **-OH from the acid** and the **-H from the alcohol group** combine to make **H2O**, and the remaining C and O join to form the **ester link, -COO-**.
bullets: -COOH + HO- → -COO- + H2O
The ester link is drawn as **-C(=O)-O-**: a carbon with a double-bonded O, joined to a single-bonded O.
One molecule of water is eliminated for **every ester link** formed.
This is the same type of reaction that joins a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to make a simple ester.
Each monomer still has a reactive group at its other end, so the chain can keep growing in both directions.

callouts.p: The OH comes from the acid and only the H comes from the diol. Do not remove both oxygens.

fig.cap: A carboxyl group on the acid reacts with a hydroxyl group on the diol. The atoms circled in red (OH from the acid and H from the diol) are lost as water, leaving an ester link (-COO-) joining the two monomers.

core.p: Because both monomers have a reactive group at **each end**, the chain grows by adding acid, diol, acid, diol in turn. The two types of monomer **alternate** in the polymer.
bullets: Acid end of one monomer joins to alcohol end of the next.
The chain is ...-acid-diol-acid-diol-... joined by ester links.
Thousands of monomers join to give a high average relative molecular mass.
Every new link releases another water molecule.
Each repeating unit contains **one acid unit and one diol unit** and two ester links (one inside, one shared at the end).

core.p: Using block diagrams, the general equation for making a polyester from n molecules of each monomer is written below. It is the most commonly examined way of showing this reaction.
bullets: **n HOOC-□-COOH + n HO-■-OH → -(OC-□-COO-■-O)n- + 2n H2O**
Each repeating unit forms **two ester links**, so **2n** water molecules are given off.
(Strictly, a chain with ends has 2n - 1 links, but **2n H2O** is accepted for very large n.)
The repeating unit starts with **-OC-** from the acid and ends with **-O-** from the diol.
Check: the repeating unit = acid + diol minus 2H2O.

callouts.p: Always write n in front of both monomers, n after the bracket, and 2n in front of H2O.

fig.cap: The repeating unit of a polyester. One acid unit (blue) and one diol unit (yellow) are joined by an ester link; the bonds pass through the brackets and n shows the unit repeats, with 2n water molecules also formed.

core.p: Exams may give real monomers. A simple example is **ethanedioic acid** with **ethane-1,2-diol**.
bullets: Acid: HOOC-COOH (ethanedioic acid).
Diol: HO-CH2-CH2-OH (ethane-1,2-diol).
Equation: **n HOOC-COOH + n HOCH2CH2OH → -(OC-COO-CH2CH2-O)n- + 2n H2O**
**PET** (poly(ethylene terephthalate)) is made from **ethane-1,2-diol** and **benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid** (terephthalic acid).
The benzene ring in PET's acid unit makes the chains rigid, giving a strong polymer.

callouts.p: PET is the polyester used for plastic drinks bottles and polyester clothing fibres.

core.h: Deducing the monomers from a polyester
core.p: To work backwards, find each **ester link (-COO-)** and split the chain there, then put back the atoms of water.
bullets: Step 1: find the ester links in the repeating unit.
Step 2: break each link between the **C=O carbon** and the **single-bonded O**.
Step 3: add **-OH** to the C=O side to make a **-COOH** group.
Step 4: add **-H** to the O side to make an **-OH** group.
The molecule with two -COOH groups is the dicarboxylic acid; the one with two -OH groups is the diol.
Check each monomer has two functional groups, one at each end.

callouts.p: The acid monomer must end up with two C=O groups; the diol has none.

core.p: This comparison is a favourite 4 to 6 mark question. Learn the differences in monomers, functional groups and products.
bullets: Addition: monomers have a **C=C**; condensation: monomers have **two functional groups** each.
Addition: usually **one** type of monomer; polyester: **two** types of monomer.
Addition: **one product** (the polymer); condensation: **two products** (polymer + water).
Addition: repeating unit has the **same atoms** as the monomer; condensation: repeating unit has **fewer atoms** than the monomers combined.
Addition: backbone of carbon only; polyester: backbone includes **oxygen atoms in ester links**.

fig.cap: In addition polymerisation identical monomers join and the polymer is the only product. In condensation polymerisation two different monomers alternate along the chain and a small molecule (water) is also formed.

core.p: Polyesters are strong and can be drawn into fibres or moulded, so they have important uses.
bullets: **Clothing and textiles**: polyester fibres are strong, hard-wearing, quick-drying and resist creasing.
**Plastic bottles (PET)**: strong, lightweight, transparent, unreactive with drinks and shatterproof.
PET is widely **recycled**, e.g. into fleece fibres or new bottles.
The ester links can be broken by **hydrolysis** (reaction with water, faster with acid or alkali), which is the reverse of the condensation reaction.
Some polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid), are **biodegradable** for this reason.

callouts.p: Do not claim all polyesters are biodegradable: PET breaks down very slowly in the environment.

core.p: Questions may ask how many water molecules form, or the formula of the repeating unit. Use the rule: **one water per ester link**.
bullets: One acid + one diol joining once: 1 H2O.
n acid + n diol forming a long chain: about 2n H2O.
Formula of repeating unit = (acid formula + diol formula) - 2 H2O.
Example: HOOC-COOH (C2H2O4) + HOCH2CH2OH (C2H6O2) = C4H8O6; minus 2H2O gives **C4H4O4**.
Mass is still conserved overall: mass of monomers = mass of polymer + mass of water.

core.h: Functional groups and the ester link
core.p: Recognising functional groups is the key skill. The reaction only involves the groups at the ends of each monomer.
bullets: **-COOH** carboxyl group (carboxylic acid).
**-OH** hydroxyl group (alcohol / diol).
**-COO-** ester link in the polymer.
The hydrocarbon or ring between the groups is unchanged in the reaction.
Polyester chains are held together by intermolecular forces; the ester groups and rings make these stronger than in poly(ethene).

callouts.p: The -COO- group formed when a carboxylic acid group reacts with an alcohol group, with the loss of water.

analogy.p: Picture a line of dancers in two teams: acid dancers wearing blue gloves on both hands and diol dancers wearing yellow gloves. A blue hand can only hold a yellow hand, so the line must go blue, yellow, blue, yellow. Every time two hands join, the dancers drop one glove each (a blue finger and a yellow finger) into a bucket: that dropped pair is the water molecule. Because everyone has two hands, the line can keep growing from both ends. The analogy breaks down because in real molecules the acid loses OH and the diol loses only H (not equal pieces), and the 'handshake' is a new covalent bond that is hard to break apart.

terms.d: Polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups join, with the elimination of a small molecule such as water.
A condensation polymer formed from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, in which the monomers are joined by ester links.
A molecule with two carboxyl (-COOH) groups.
A molecule with two hydroxyl (-OH) groups.
The -COOH functional group of carboxylic acids.
The -OH functional group of alcohols.
The -COO- group joining monomers in a polyester.
An atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic reactions of a molecule.
A small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer.
The part of a polymer that repeats along the chain, shown in brackets with n.
Removal of a small molecule, such as water, during a reaction.
A polyester made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, used for bottles and fibres.
The diol HO-CH2-CH2-OH, a common polyester monomer.
Breaking a bond by reaction with water; breaks ester links and reverses condensation.
Polymerisation of monomers with a C=C double bond, giving the polymer as the only product.

mistakes.w: A polyester is made from one type of monomer with a double bond.
mistakes.r: A polyester is made from two monomers, a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, by condensation polymerisation.

mistakes.w: Condensation polymerisation gives only the polymer.
mistakes.r: It gives the polymer and a small molecule, water.

mistakes.w: The diol has two -COOH groups.
mistakes.r: A diol has two -OH groups; the dicarboxylic acid has two -COOH groups.

mistakes.w: Writes n H2O in the polyester equation.
mistakes.r: Two ester links form per repeating unit, so 2n H2O.

mistakes.w: Draws the ester link as -CO-, -O-O- or -COOH-.
mistakes.r: The ester link is -COO-, a C=O with a single-bonded O.

mistakes.w: Removes OH from both monomers to make water.
mistakes.r: OH is removed from the acid and H from the alcohol group.

mistakes.w: Monomers in condensation polymerisation need one functional group.
mistakes.r: Each monomer needs two functional groups so the chain can grow at both ends.

mistakes.w: Polyesters and addition polymers have the same atoms in the repeat unit as the monomers.
mistakes.r: Only addition polymers do; a polyester repeating unit has lost 2H2O compared with the monomers.

exam.q: State the type of polymerisation used to make polyesters.
model: condensation (polymerisation)
exam.tip: Spell condensation carefully.

exam.q: Name the two types of monomer used to make a polyester.
model: a dicarboxylic acid
a diol
exam.tip: 'Acid and alcohol' alone may not score; use 'di' terms.

exam.q: Name the small molecule formed when a polyester is made.
model: water / H2O
exam.tip: For polyesters it is always water.

exam.q: Give the formula of the functional group in a dicarboxylic acid and in a diol.
model: -COOH (carboxyl)
-OH (hydroxyl)
exam.tip: Write the group, not the whole molecule.

exam.q: Complete the equation: n HOOC-□-COOH + n HO-■-OH → ... + ...
model: -(OC-□-COO-■-O)n- with bonds through brackets
2n H2O
exam.tip: Two marks: one for the repeat unit, one for 2n H2O.

exam.q: A polyester has the repeating unit -(OC-C6H4-COO-CH2CH2-O)n-. Give the structures of the two monomers.
model: HOOC-C6H4-COOH
HO-CH2CH2-OH
exam.tip: Add OH to the C=O ends and H to the O ends.

exam.q: Explain why each monomer used to make a polyester must have two functional groups.
model: so each monomer can react / join at both ends
allowing a long chain to form (one group would end the chain)
exam.tip: Link the structure to chain growth.

exam.q: Explain why polyesters are described as condensation polymers.
model: monomers join together
with the loss/elimination of a small molecule (water) each time a link forms
exam.tip: Mention the small molecule by name.

exam.q: Give two uses of polyesters.
model: clothing / textile fibres
plastic drinks bottles (PET)
exam.tip: Any two sensible uses.

exam.q: Compare addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. [6 marks]
model: addition monomers contain a C=C double bond
condensation monomers have two functional groups each, e.g. -COOH and -OH
addition usually uses one type of monomer, polyesters use two (dicarboxylic acid and diol)
addition gives the polymer only
condensation gives the polymer and a small molecule (water)
polyester monomers are joined by ester links; addition polymers by C-C bonds formed when the double bond opens
exam.tip: Write in pairs of comparisons using 'whereas' so each point is clearly linked.

worked.q: Write the equation for the formation of a polyester from ethanedioic acid, HOOC-COOH, and ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH.
steps: Identify groups: the acid has two -COOH, the diol has two -OH.
Each -COOH joins an -OH: remove OH from the acid and H from the diol, forming H2O.
Repeating unit: -OC-COO-CH2CH2-O-, drawn in brackets with n.
Two ester links per repeating unit, so 2n H2O.
worked.ans: n HOOC-COOH + n HOCH2CH2OH → -(OC-COO-CH2CH2-O)n- + 2n H2O

worked.q: Work out the molecular formula of the repeating unit in the polyester made from HOOC-COOH and HOCH2CH2OH.
steps: Acid formula: C2H2O4.
Diol formula: C2H6O2.
Add them: C4H8O6.
Two water molecules are lost per repeating unit: subtract 2H2O = H4O2.
C4H8O6 - H4O2 = C4H4O4
worked.ans: C4H4O4

worked.q: A polyester chain contains 500 acid units and 500 diol units. Estimate the number of water molecules formed.
steps: Each ester link releases one H2O.
Units alternate: 1000 monomers in a chain have 999 links.
So 999 water molecules form, which is about 2n = 1000 where n = 500.
For very large chains 2n H2O is used in the equation.
worked.ans: 999 molecules of water (approximately 2n = 1000).

chem_edx.9.9.summary: Most polymers (plastics) are made from **crude oil**, a **finite resource**, and most are **non-biodegradable**, so they stay in landfill sites for hundreds of years. Burning polymers releases energy but also produces **carbon dioxide** (a greenhouse gas) and, for some polymers such as PVC, **toxic gases** like hydrogen chloride; incomplete combustion can also make carbon monoxide and soot. **Recycling** saves crude oil, reduces landfill and reduces the gases released by burning, but it costs money and energy to collect, sort and process plastics, so you must be able to **evaluate** both sides using economic, environmental and resource arguments.

core.p: Addition polymers such as poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC and PTFE are made from small alkene monomers. These monomers are produced by **cracking** fractions from **crude oil**, so almost every everyday plastic depends on crude oil as its **starting material**.
bullets: Crude oil is a **finite (non-renewable) resource**: it formed over millions of years and is being used up far faster than it forms.
Crude oil is also needed for fuels (petrol, diesel, kerosene) and as a feedstock for many other chemicals, so plastics compete with these uses.
As crude oil runs out it will become **scarcer and more expensive**, so new polymer will cost more to make.
This is the first spec problem: the **availability of starting materials**.
Some polymers can be made from plant-based (renewable) starting materials, but most plastics in use today still come from crude oil.

callouts.p: Most polymers are made from crude oil, which is a finite resource, so the starting materials will become less available and more expensive.

core.h: Why polymers are so useful in the first place
core.p: To evaluate disposal you need to understand why we use so much plastic. Polymers are cheap, light, strong, easily moulded, waterproof and **unreactive**. That last property is exactly what causes the disposal problem.
bullets: Polymers are made of very long chains held by strong **covalent bonds** within each chain.
They do not react with water, air, most acids or most microorganisms under normal conditions.
This makes them great for food packaging, water pipes, bottles and electrical insulation.
But the same **unreactivity** means they do not break down when thrown away.
Many plastic items are designed to be used once (single-use packaging), so large amounts reach the waste stream quickly.

callouts.t: Link the property to the problem
callouts.p: Top answers say: polymers are unreactive, so microorganisms cannot break them down, so they are non-biodegradable and persist in landfill.

core.p: Most addition polymers are **non-biodegradable**: decomposers (bacteria and fungi) cannot digest the long hydrocarbon chains. When plastic waste is buried in **landfill sites** it can stay there for hundreds of years.
bullets: **Biodegradable** means able to be broken down by microorganisms.
Landfill sites take up **large areas of land** that could be used for other things.
As landfill sites fill up, **new sites must be found**, which is increasingly difficult and expensive.
Plastic waste that escapes landfill (litter) harms wildlife: animals can swallow it or become trapped.
Plastics slowly break into smaller pieces (microplastics) but this is not biodegradation: the polymer itself remains.
Landfill sites can be unsightly and cause local smells and pests (from the other waste buried with plastic).

callouts.p: Cannot be broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria, so it persists in the environment for a very long time.
Polymers persist in landfill sites because they are non-biodegradable.

core.h: Problem: gases produced when polymers are burned
core.p: Burning (**incineration**) gets rid of plastic and the heat released can be used to generate electricity. However, combustion of polymers produces gases that cause problems.
bullets: Polymers containing carbon and hydrogen burn to give **carbon dioxide and water** in complete combustion.
**Carbon dioxide** is a **greenhouse gas** that contributes to global warming and climate change.

If oxygen is limited, **incomplete combustion** produces **carbon monoxide** (toxic: it binds to haemoglobin and reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen) and **carbon particulates (soot)**, which can cause breathing problems and global dimming.

Polymers containing other elements give extra toxic gases. **PVC**, poly(chloroethene), contains chlorine, so burning it releases **hydrogen chloride**, HCl, which is toxic and forms hydrochloric acid in moist air (contributing to acid rain).
Burning plastic destroys the material, so the crude oil used to make it is lost for good.
Modern incinerators need expensive filters and scrubbers to remove harmful gases from the waste gases.

head: Gas or product
When it forms
Why it is a problem
rows: Complete combustion of any carbon-based polymer
Greenhouse gas, linked to climate change
Toxic: reduces oxygen carried by the blood

callouts.p: Burning polymers produces toxic gases, for example hydrogen chloride from PVC and carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion, as well as carbon dioxide.

callouts.t: Do not say all polymers make HCl
callouts.p: Only polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, produce hydrogen chloride. Poly(ethene) burns to carbon dioxide and water (or CO and soot if oxygen is limited).

core.p: There are three main ways to deal with waste polymers: **landfill**, **incineration (combustion)** and **recycling**. Each has advantages and disadvantages and exam questions often ask you to compare them.
bullets: Landfill is cheap and simple but wastes land and the polymer persists.
Incineration reduces the volume of waste and can generate electricity, but releases CO2 and possibly toxic gases.
Recycling saves crude oil and reduces landfill and emissions, but needs collection, sorting and energy.
No method is perfect, so the best choice depends on the type of polymer, local facilities and cost.

head: Method
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Uses land; non-biodegradable polymer persists; crude oil wasted
Reduces waste volume; heat can generate electricity
CO2 (greenhouse gas); toxic gases such as HCl and CO; crude oil lost
Saves crude oil; less landfill; fewer gases from burning; often less energy than making new polymer
Collection, sorting, washing cost money and energy; polymers must be separated; quality can fall each cycle

core.p: In **mechanical recycling** used plastic is collected, **sorted by polymer type**, cleaned, shredded into flakes, melted and remoulded into new products.
bullets: **Collection**: from households and businesses, needs lorries, fuel and workers.
**Sorting**: different polymers must be separated because they have different melting points and properties; a mixture gives poor-quality plastic.
Many plastics carry a **recycling code** (numbers 1 to 7 in a triangle) to help sorting.
**Washing**: food and labels must be removed.
**Shredding** into small flakes or pellets.
**Melting and remoulding** into new items such as fleece clothing, pipes, crates or new bottles.
Each time a polymer is recycled, the chains can be damaged, so the quality may fall; it can only be recycled a limited number of times.

callouts.p: Different polymers have different melting points and are often not compatible when melted together, so unsorted plastic gives a weak, low-value product. Sorting is the most expensive and labour-intensive step.

core.p: Recycling tackles all three spec problems at once: starting materials, landfill and gases from burning.
bullets: **Conserves crude oil**: less new polymer needs to be made, so the finite resource lasts longer.
**Reduces landfill**: less non-biodegradable waste is buried, so landfill sites fill more slowly.
**Reduces gases from combustion**: less plastic is burned, so less CO2 and fewer toxic gases are released.
Often **uses less energy** than making new polymer from crude oil (no extraction, fractional distillation, cracking and polymerisation needed), which also means less CO2 from burning fuels.
Can create jobs and income from selling recycled material.
Reduces litter and harm to wildlife.

callouts.p: Recycling saves starting materials (crude oil), reduces persistence in landfill and reduces gases produced during disposal by combustion.

core.h: Disadvantages of recycling polymers (including economic issues)
core.p: Recycling is not free. The **economic issues** are a key part of 9.24C: if recycling costs more than making new plastic, it may not happen without government support.
bullets: **Collection costs**: transport, fuel and staff; lorries burning fuel also release CO2.
**Sorting costs**: different polymers must be separated, often by hand or with expensive machinery.
**Cleaning** uses water and energy.
**Energy is still needed** to melt and remould the polymer.
The recycled polymer is often **lower quality**, so it sells for a lower price and is used for less demanding products.
When crude oil is cheap, **new polymer can be cheaper than recycled polymer**, so recycling may be uneconomic.
Some polymers (for example many mixed or thin films, and thermosetting polymers) are difficult or impossible to recycle.
Relies on people sorting their rubbish correctly at home.

callouts.p: Collection lorries, sorting plants and melting all use energy, often from burning fossil fuels, so recycling still releases some carbon dioxide. It usually releases less than making new polymer, but not none.

core.h: Evaluating recycling: building a balanced answer
core.p: An **evaluate** question wants arguments for and against, then a **justified conclusion**. Use the three spec headings as a checklist: **economic issues**, **gases produced during disposal by combustion**, and **availability of starting materials**.
bullets: Start with an advantage, explained: recycling means less crude oil is used, which is important because crude oil is finite.
Give a second advantage: less plastic is burned, so less CO2 (greenhouse gas) and fewer toxic gases such as HCl from PVC.
Give a third: less waste goes to landfill, where non-biodegradable polymers persist.
Then disadvantages: collecting and sorting cost money and energy; recycled polymer can be lower quality; may be more expensive than new polymer.
Conclude: for example, recycling is worthwhile overall because it conserves a finite resource and reduces pollution, provided the polymers can be sorted efficiently.
Use data if the question gives it, and quote numbers from the table or graph.

callouts.p: Aim for three linked advantages, two or three linked disadvantages and a conclusion that weighs them. Each point should say what happens AND why it matters.

core.p: Edexcel often gives a table of energy used, cost or emissions for making new polymer versus recycled polymer. You must **use the figures** to support your judgement.
bullets: Calculate differences or percentages when asked, for example energy saved = energy for new polymer minus energy for recycled polymer.
Comment on whether the difference is large or small.
Link energy saving to reduced fuel use and lower CO2 emissions.
Look for limitations in the data: does it include collection and transport? Is it only for one type of polymer?
Do not just copy numbers: say what they show.

core.h: Reducing the problems in other ways
core.p: Recycling is only one solution. Others link to the same spec ideas and can earn credit in extended answers.
bullets: **Reduce**: use less plastic, for example by charging for carrier bags.
**Reuse**: use plastic items several times before disposal.
Use **biodegradable polymers** for some uses, which microorganisms can break down.
Burn waste plastic in incinerators that **generate electricity** and have **scrubbers** to remove acidic gases like HCl.
Develop polymers made from **renewable** plant-based starting materials.

core.p: Mark schemes reward specific words. Make sure your answers include them.
bullets: **finite / non-renewable** resource (crude oil)
**non-biodegradable** and **persist** in landfill
**toxic** gases, **hydrogen chloride** from PVC, **carbon monoxide** from incomplete combustion
**carbon dioxide** is a **greenhouse gas**
**sorting** and **collection** costs
**conserves** crude oil, **reduces** landfill
**evaluate** needs a **conclusion**

analogy.t: Plastic is like a glitter spill
analogy.p: Glitter is cheap, bright and useful, but once it is spread around it is almost impossible to get rid of: it does not dissolve or rot away (non-biodegradable, persisting like plastic in landfill). You could set fire to it, but that makes smoke (like toxic gases from burning). Collecting and sorting it to reuse is possible but slow and fiddly (the cost of collecting and sorting for recycling). The analogy breaks down because glitter is not usually made from a finite resource that is running out, and burning real plastic in a modern incinerator can usefully generate electricity.

terms.d: A very large molecule made from many small repeating units (monomers) joined together.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
A finite mixture of hydrocarbons that is the main source of the starting materials for most polymers.
A resource that is being used up faster than it can be replaced, so it will run out.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
Cannot be broken down by microorganisms, so persists in the environment.
A large hole in the ground where waste is buried.
Disposal of waste by burning (combustion); the heat can be used to generate electricity.
Burning in plenty of oxygen; hydrocarbons produce carbon dioxide and water.
Burning in limited oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
A toxic, acidic gas, HCl, released when PVC is burned.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that absorbs heat radiated from the Earth, contributing to global warming.
Processing used materials so they can be made into new products.
Separating waste polymers into their different types so they can be recycled.
Poly(chloroethene), an addition polymer containing chlorine, used for pipes, window frames and cable insulation.
Costs and benefits in money, for example the cost of collecting and sorting compared with the price of new polymer.

mistakes.w: Plastics are bad because they are toxic.
mistakes.r: Most polymers are unreactive and non-toxic in use; the problems are that they are non-biodegradable, made from finite crude oil, and can give toxic gases when burned.

mistakes.w: Plastics take a long time to biodegrade so they rot slowly in landfill.
mistakes.r: Most addition polymers are non-biodegradable: microorganisms cannot break them down, so they persist in landfill.

mistakes.w: Burning all plastics releases chlorine gas.
mistakes.r: Burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride (HCl), because PVC contains chlorine. Other polymers like poly(ethene) do not.

mistakes.w: Recycling plastic uses no energy and has no cost.
mistakes.r: Collecting, transporting, sorting, washing and melting all cost money and use energy, but usually less energy than making new polymer.

mistakes.w: Recycling saves fossil fuels so it stops global warming.
mistakes.r: Recycling reduces crude oil use and reduces CO2 emissions from making and burning polymers; it does not stop global warming on its own.

mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide is toxic.
mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas linked to climate change; carbon monoxide is the toxic gas from incomplete combustion.

mistakes.w: An evaluation lists advantages and disadvantages only.
mistakes.r: Evaluate questions need a justified conclusion that weighs the points.

mistakes.w: Plastics can be recycled forever.
mistakes.r: The polymer chains degrade and quality falls, so a polymer can only be recycled a limited number of times.

mistakes.w: Different plastics can all be melted down together.
mistakes.r: Polymers must be sorted by type because they have different properties and melting points.

exam.q: Give one reason why the starting materials for making poly(ethene) will become less available in the future.
model: They come from crude oil, which is a finite / non-renewable resource.
exam.tip: Name crude oil AND say finite or non-renewable.

exam.q: Explain why disposing of poly(propene) in landfill sites is a problem.
model: Poly(propene) is non-biodegradable / cannot be broken down by microorganisms.
So it persists for a very long time and landfill sites fill up / land is used up.
exam.tip: Two marks means a statement and a consequence.

exam.q: PVC waste can be disposed of by burning. State the name of a toxic gas formed and explain why it forms.
model: Hydrogen chloride (HCl).
Because PVC contains chlorine atoms.
exam.tip: Hydrogen chloride, not chlorine.

exam.q: Explain why burning plastics in a limited supply of air is particularly harmful.
model: Incomplete combustion occurs, producing carbon monoxide.
Carbon monoxide is toxic / reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen (or soot causes breathing problems).
exam.tip: Limited air is the cue for incomplete combustion.

exam.q: Give two advantages of recycling polymers rather than burning them.
model: Conserves crude oil / less new polymer needed.
Fewer gases released, e.g. less CO2 or no toxic HCl.
exam.tip: Compare with burning, as the question asks.

exam.q: Give two reasons why recycling polymers can be expensive.
model: Polymers must be collected and transported.
Different polymers must be sorted / separated (and washed).
exam.tip: These are the economic issues named in the spec.

exam.q: Suggest why recycled polymer is often used for lower-value products than new polymer.
model: Polymer chains are damaged / properties change during recycling or mixtures may be present.
So recycled polymer is lower quality / weaker.
exam.tip: Link quality to value.

exam.q: Explain why incineration of polymer waste can be better than landfill but still causes environmental problems.
model: Incineration reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill.
Heat released can be used to generate electricity.
But carbon dioxide is released, which is a greenhouse gas / causes climate change.
And toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride (from PVC) or carbon monoxide may be released.
exam.tip: Balance two benefits with two problems.

exam.q: A company makes 1000 tonnes of new poly(ethene) using 80 000 GJ of energy. Recycling 1000 tonnes uses 20 000 GJ. Calculate the percentage of energy saved by recycling.
model: Energy saved = 80 000 - 20 000 = 60 000 GJ.
Percentage saved = 60 000 / 80 000 x 100 = 75%.
exam.tip: Divide by the original (new polymer) value.

exam.q: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of recycling polymers. Your answer should refer to economic issues, gases produced during disposal and the availability of starting materials.
model: Recycling reduces the amount of crude oil needed, which is a finite resource, so it lasts longer.
Making recycled polymer often uses less energy than making new polymer, saving fuel and money.
Less polymer is burned, so less carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) is released.
Less burning means fewer toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride from PVC or carbon monoxide.
Less waste goes to landfill, where non-biodegradable polymers persist.
However, collecting, transporting and sorting polymers costs money and uses energy.
Recycled polymer may be lower quality, and may cost more than new polymer when oil is cheap.
Conclusion: recycling is worthwhile overall because it conserves finite resources and reduces pollution, provided sorting is efficient.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs a balanced, linked argument with a justified conclusion covering all three named areas.

worked.q: Data: making 1 kg of new PET from crude oil uses 84 MJ of energy; recycling 1 kg of PET uses 30 MJ. Use the data to evaluate whether PET should be recycled.
steps: Find the energy saved: 84 - 30 = 54 MJ per kg.
Percentage saved: 54 / 84 x 100 = 64% (to 2 significant figures).
Interpret: recycling uses much less energy, so less fuel is burned and less CO2 is released.
Add a resource point: recycling also reduces the amount of crude oil needed, a finite resource.
Add a limitation: the data may not include the energy used to collect and sort the PET.
Conclude with a judgement.
worked.ans: Recycling PET saves about 64% of the energy, so it reduces fuel use, CO2 emissions and crude oil use; overall it should be recycled, although collection and sorting costs (possibly not included in the data) reduce the benefit.

worked.q: A council must choose between landfill and incineration for mixed plastic waste that contains some PVC. Write a model comparison.
steps: Landfill: cheap and no harmful gases from burning, but the plastics are non-biodegradable so they persist and use up land.
Incineration: reduces waste volume and can generate electricity.
But burning releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.
The PVC contains chlorine, so burning it releases toxic, acidic hydrogen chloride; scrubbers would be needed, which cost money.
Neither option conserves crude oil; the waste polymer is lost.
Judgement: incineration with energy recovery and gas cleaning is better for land use, but sorting out PVC for recycling first would reduce toxic gas.
worked.ans: Incineration saves landfill space and recovers energy but releases CO2 and HCl from PVC; landfill avoids gases but wastes land as plastics persist. Best overall: remove PVC and recyclable polymers first, then incinerate the rest with energy recovery and gas scrubbing.

svg.cap: The life of a polymer. Crude oil (finite) is cracked to make monomers, which are polymerised and made into products. After use there are three disposal routes: landfill (the polymer persists), incineration (releases CO2 and possibly toxic gases) or recycling, which loops material back and reduces the need for new crude oil.
